title: 1.Environmental variables driving diversity of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in Ohio soybean agricultural systems.
abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) play a crucial role in crop productivity and agroecosystem processes. However, the composition of soil AMF communities and the factors controlling their diversity and distribution in Ohio remain poorly understood. We profiled soil AMF and physico-chemical characteristics in 17 soybean fields across agricultural regions in Ohio. Mycorrhizal fungi were recovered through amplicon sequencing of the 18S ribosomal gene coupled with PacBio technology. Within Glomeromycota, we detected 14 genera belonging to six families. The familyGlomeraceaeaccounted for >50% of the AMF reads recovered, while the families Gigasporaceae and Archaeosporaceae were rare. At the genus level,Entrophospora,Nanoglomus,Paraglomus, andFunneliformiswere most widespread, contrasting with rare taxa such asGigaspora,Dominikia, andArchaeospora. Soil AMF community composition varied across soil pH ranges (5.2-7.7), with most genera observed in soils with pH between 5.5-6.5.Funneliformis,Entrophospora, andDiversisporawere present in soils with a wide pH range, but their highest abundance was observed in soils with slightly alkaline conditions, whileGigasporaandArchaeosporawere present in soils with near-neutral pH. From the 17 fields studied, eight were infested with soybean cyst nematode (SCN), with densities ranging from 40 to 720 eggs per 100 cm3of soil. In these soils, AMF diversity was negatively correlated with SCN abundance, and some specific AMF genera were associated with OM, TEC and P. Future research should expand soil sampling to root colonization and evaluate functional impacts on soybean yields in Ohio.

title: 2.A dynamic model of complex plant infections based on a continuum of pathogenesis strategies: verification using long-term spring wheat data under climatic aridification.
abstract: Current epidemiological models predominantly treat plant pathogens as discrete taxonomic entities, largely ignoring the dynamic and continuous nature of their ecological strategies. This study proposes a novel theoretical framework that integrates the Ramensky-Grime CSR continuum concept into phytopathology, representing pathogenesis strategies not as fixed categories, but as vectors in a continuous L-J-T space bounded by three archetypes: active immune breaching (L-strategy), exergy exploitation (J-strategy), and baseline erosion (T-strategy). Three mechanisms governing transitions within this continuum are introduced: ontogenetic shift, phenotypic plasticity, and evolutionary adaptation. The host's physiological potential (V) is modeled as a function of negative entropy (Bauer's principle), and disease progression is framed as a stochastic optimization problem using Bellman dynamics. The model is verified against a unique 32-year (1992-2024) dataset on spring wheat pathosystem dynamics in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russian Federation. The dataset documents a climate-driven shift in the pathogen community centroid from an L-dominated to a J/T-dominated state, consistent with model predictions. The framework provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed rise of necrotrophic and soil-borne pathogens under aridification and offers a mathematical basis for predicting long-term shifts in phytosanitary risk.

title: 3.Climate-induced shocks, food insecurity and strategies for tackling evolving impacts within the Alliance of Sahel States.
abstract: This study sought to analyse and quantify the impacts of floods (proxy through positive rainfall anomalies) and droughts (negative rainfall anomalies) on household food security in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), namely Burkina Faso, Mali and niger. These countries are also designated crisis countries by the FAO. The goal of the study was to determine and recommend to the countries' governments, the FAO and other development partners, pathways to buffering vulnerable households' food security against climate -induced shocks. The specific objectives of the study were to: 1) Assess how positive and negative rainfall shocks affect food security in the AES, and 2) Explore and recommend available strategies needed to enhance resilience, support adaptation and reduce food insecurity in these states. Two datasets, household survey and satellite precipitation data, were used for the analysis. The household survey data was obtained from the FAO DIEM household survey database, while the precipitation data was extracted from the ECMWF Climate Reanalysis v5 (ERA5) high, spatiotemporal resolution monthly precipitation data provided by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), Copernicus Climate Change Services. The FAO-DIEM data contains information on various food security indicators. The study however, focused on three of these food security indicators, namely the Food Consumption Score (FCS), the Reduced Coping Strategy Index (rCSI) and Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES). The multiple linear regression model was used to estimate the effects of positive and negative rainfall anomalies on household food security. From the analysis, the following conclusions can be drawn: 1) Both positive rainfall anomalies and droughts threaten food security within the AES. While the incidence of floods is disruptive in the short term with implications for food production, droughts cause long term food production risks and livelihood stress. Unlike droughts the incidence and effects of which unfold gradually, the incidence of floods is sudden. Thus, adjusting to the sudden shocks of flood effects is more difficult than adjusting to the gradual effects of droughts. The fast-track nature of flood incidence may imply difficulties for households to adequately ex-ante coping measures. This way, ex-post flood damages may be more deleterious that those of droughts. 2) Crop-livestock diversification is associated with reduced vulnerability and improved household resilience and food security. Thus, the adoption of livestock-crop diversification strategies could be used to spread and reduce the risks associated with floods and droughts. Moreover, crop livestock diversification appears to be useful for sustaining and smoothening household consumption and income patterns to provide a stronger buffer against food insecurity and improve the quality of diets and nutrition among households. Generally, food insecurity interventions, namely cash, food, and asset support, are expected to serve as swift and targeted responses to crises, while linking social protection to nutrition and overall household welfare. Addressing the bottlenecks to food security and consolidating the gains from the social protection divide could be the beginning of safeguarding food supplies, protecting rural economies and ensuring the sustainability of food systems in crisis communities. Based on the above conclusions, the following recommendations are provided to guide the actions of governments of the AES countries, FAO and other development interest groups: 1) In the short term, there is the need for integrated support systems such as cash and asset support as well as targeted food reliefs under more severe situations. This is critical as it addresses the very immediate hunger and potential food insecurity problems while protecting livelihoods. It also, supports and builds seasonal and shock responsive programming whilst strengthening local markets, targeting and protecting the very vulnerable in the society as well as building the adaptive capacities of communities to climate shocks. 2) In the medium term, we recommend the promotion of crop-livestock diversification across the AES. The promotion of crop-livestock diversification is a sure bet to stabilising and smoothing households' income and food supply. This intervention will help bridge seasonal food shortage gaps within households and prevent them from impulse sales of assets. Additionally, the economic viability of households would be enhanced with more market participation due to the benefits and cross-effects of integrating crops and livestock. 3) In the long, there is the need to strengthen flood preparedness and rapid response mechanisms. The importance of this cannot be overstated as this could build the long-term resilience of households and communities to reduce repeated displacements caused by floods and droughts. Also, strengthening flood preparedness and rapid response mechanisms would preserve development gains and thus ensure that resources are channelled to other equally pressing developmental needs. These would save lives in the now and protect livelihoods and developmental gains for the future.

title: 4.Drought by design? How rainfall data choices shape food insecurity estimates.
abstract: This study combines household survey data from Mali and Chad with ten rainfall datasets from various sources to examine how the choice of rainfall data influences estimates of drought impacts on food security. Rainfall shocks are measured using the Standardized Precipitation Index and assigned through bilinear, nearest-neighbor, and zonal aggregation techniques. Results without controls reveal substantial heterogeneity. Estimated coefficients vary widely in both magnitude and sign across datasets and interpolation methods, with coarse or satellite-only products exhibiting particularly high volatility. Once controls are added, this heterogeneity largely disappears and coefficients converge toward consistently negative values in line with theoretical expectations. Beyond magnitudes, the analysis also finds that the relative ranking of datasets shifts depending on the interpolation method and model specification, revealing instability in dataset performance. The findings highlight a fundamental challenge for applied economics since empirical conclusions may depend as much on dataset choice, spatial interpolation, and specification decisions as on the underlying relationship. This highlights the importance of transparency in the selection and processing of rainfall data.

title: 5.Emergence and spatial redistribution of severe Dalaca pallens infestations across western Patagonian pastures.
abstract: Recent severe infestations ofDalaca pallensin western Patagonia suggest a shift in the spatial distribution of this key pasture pest beyond its historically recognized range. Larval infestation was quantified across agroecological gradients in the Ays'en region (Chile) using a multivariate framework in which 2025 observations were projected onto a reference space defined using 2021 data, enabling direct comparison within a fixed environmental structure. The 2021 configuration showed a strong concentration of infestation within a restricted sector of the gradient. By contrast, the 2025 projection revealed a broader spatial footprint and a marked redistribution of infestation intensity across environmental sectors, including increased representation in previously secondary areas. This shift was accompanied by a consistent displacement of the infestation core toward more continental and higher-elevation conditions. Although causal mechanisms cannot be established, the observed pattern is consistent with a reorganization of infestation patterns across the regional environmental gradient under changing conditions. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence of severeD. pallensoutbreaks in western Patagonia and establish a baseline for future studies integrating climatic and phenological drivers.

title: 6.The impact of floods on food insecurity and vulnerability in Democratic Republic of the Congo.
abstract: I study the impacts of floods on household food insecurity and vulnerability in Democratic Republic of the Congo. I combine household-level data with two measures of exposure to floods, self-reported exposure and an objective indicator of large flood events at territory-level. I exploit territory-level variation in timing of exposure to floods combined with exposure to floods to identify causal impacts. I find that self-reported exposure to flood is associated with higher food insecurity and greater reliance on negative coping strategies. In contrast, causal estimates based on an objective measure of exposure to floods suggest that exposure to floods does not significantly change consumption frequency or dietary diversity but is associated with improved food security in Eastern DRC. I explore whether this pattern is driven by short-run economic activity or increased agricultural production and find suggestive evidence that exposure to floods in this context expand cultivated land.

title: 7.A web-based digital seed viability nomograph for interactive estimation of seed longevity from moisture content, temperature, and storage duration.
abstract: Reliable estimation of seed longevity is central to agriculture, seed banking, restoration, and plant genetic resource conservation. For orthodox seeds, the Ellis-Roberts viability framework remains one of the most influential quantitative approaches for relating storage life to seed moisture content, temperature, and initial seed quality. Classical seed nomographs translated this framework into practical graphical tools, but many contemporary users now work in digital environments and require interactive, portable, and transparent decision-support tools. Here, we present a browser accessible digital seed viability nomograph, implemented as a React/Vite web application and available at https://seed-viability-nomograph.vercel.app. The tool allows users to adjust seed moisture content, storage temperature, storage duration, and viability constants, and then visualizes predicted germination decline, time to selected viability thresholds, and a moisture-based nomograph table. The application is intended as a teaching, research-prototyping, and planning interface rather than as a substitute for species-specific experimental calibration. This distinction is important because orthodox, intermediate, and recalcitrant seeds differ fundamentally in storage biology, and conventional dry seed models are most appropriate for orthodox materials. The digital implementation modernizes classical longevity theory through a portable and transparent interface that can be accessed directly in a web browser, making seed viability prediction easier to explore, communicate, and adapt for educational and preliminary analytical use.

title: 8.Anomalous temporal synchronization in U.S. HPAI H5N1 outbreak data: evidence for uncharacterized transmission vectors in commercial poultry infrastructure.
abstract: We report the identification of an anomalous temporal synchronization pattern in USDA APHIS confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 detection data from U.S. commercial and backyard poultry flocks (February 2022-March 2026). Analysis of 672 confirmed detections revealed 160 outbreak events distributed across 12 or more states occurring within identical 48-hour windows. This synchronization velocity exceeds all established transmission mechanisms, including wild bird migration (2-4 weeks), interstate poultry trade (3-7 days), and personnel movement (1-3 days). The pattern was identified alongside seven additional structural findings, including subclinical viral persistence in urban live bird markets, a breeder-to-production supply chain transmission cascade, and mammalian spillover acceleration at eight times historical rates. We present these findings as evidence that anthropogenic transmission vectors, potentially including shared feed supply chains, equipment vendor networks, or rendering truck routes, may play a larger role in domestic H5N1 propagation than currently recognized. All results were deterministic and reproducible across three independent analytical runs.

title: 9.First record of Hercinothrips dimidiatus Hood, 1937 (Thysanoptera: Thripidae), in the United States and its pest status on Aloe L.
10.Evaluating integrated soybean cyst nematode management using spatially informed mixed models.
abstract: Evaluating management strategies for soybean cyst nematode (SCN) under field conditions remains challenging because the pathogen's inherently patchy spatial distribution inflates experimental error and can obscure treatment effects. This study combined spatially explicit linear mixed models with a split-plot field evaluation of two SCN-resistance sources (PI 88788 and Peking) and fluopyram seed treatment against nematode populations capable of reproducing on both resistance sources in Ohio. Six models spanning a gradient of spatial complexity were compared; tensor-product penalized spline models improved experimental efficiency by 33-39% relative to conventional non-spatial models. Peking-derived cultivars outperformed PI 88788 by 257 kg ha-1and suppressed nematode reproduction by 36%, demonstrating a clear advantage under these SCN population conditions. However, Peking exhibited slightly greater yield sensitivity to increasing initial SCN population density (Pi; -5.1% per log-unit increase) than PI 88788 (-4%), revealing a trade-off between reproductive suppression and yield stability. Fluopyram seed treatment increased yield by 111 kg ha-1but did not reduce SCN reproduction factor, indicating a yield-protective effect rather than direct suppression of nematode population growth. These results demonstrate that effective management in fields with populations capable of reproducing on both resistance sources requires diversification of resistance, with Peking-derived cultivars representing an important complement to PI 88788 and seed treatments providing supplementary yield protection. The spatial modeling framework developed here provides a template for improving precision in soilborne pathogen research.

title: 11.Agroecological vineyard management in cool semi-continental systems: effects on pesticide use, yield, and mildew damage.
abstract: Conventional agriculture, including viticulture, is heavily reliant on chemical inputs, and especially synthetic pesticides. However, pesticides come with unintended negative impacts for the environment and society. Agricultural systems, including vineyard, must find ways to maintain production levels while reducing pesticides to improve environmental and social outcomes. In this long-term study, we assessed various agroecological vineyard management strategies and their impacts on pesticide use, mildew control, and yield. We worked closely with key stakeholders to develop a set of 11 low-input vineyard plots implementing several combinations of technical and management changes to reduce pesticide use. The implemented changes were categorized based on the efficiency-substitution-redesign framework, and the vineyards were monitored and assessed over six consecutive years as a proof of concept. Pesticide use was successfully reduced in each of the case study plots, with most of the combinations of agroecological changes resulting in lower pesticide use while still achieving yields that both aligned with regional averages and met winegrowers' yield targets. The low-input plots produced the expected yields for six consecutive years, with acceptable levels of powdery and downy mildew damage at harvest. Our results can support the transition toward low-input vineyard systems by providing agricultural advisers with information to aid implementation and reassuring farmers who may be reluctant to make a shift to these systems.

title: 12.Soil and cocoa bean nutrients, cadmium, and market-relevant bean attributes across Papua New Guinea.
abstract: Cocoa is Papua New Guinea's (PNG) third-largest agricultural export, supporting about two million smallholder farmers. Recent cadmium (Cd) regulations in chocolate products and limits on Cd in soils pose possible risks to the sustainability of PNG's cocoa industry. This study provides the first nationwide assessment of Cd in cocoa-growing soils and cocoa beans in PNG, assesses soil nutrient status, evaluates the suitability of portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) for rapid soil Cd screening, and examines select cocoa bean attributes of market concern. A total of 122 soil samples were collected and analysed from eight cocoa-growing provinces and the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (ARoB), along with 71 cocoa bean samples from two of these provinces and ARoB. Across all provinces and ARoB, DTPA-extractable soil Cd (proxy for bioavailable Cd) averaged 0.13 mg kg-1(± 0.33 Standard Deviation). While no samples exceeded international limits (>3.0 mg kg-1), one sample from New Ireland contained 2.43 mg kg-1of Cd, indicating the need for further targeted sampling to determine the extent and spatial distribution of high Cd concentrations. At the low DTPA-extractable Cd concentrations measured across PNG, pXRF lacked the sensitivity required for reliable detection and therefore is not recommended for screening. Bean Cd concentrations were not of concern. However, all samples exceeded industry thresholds for free fatty acids (FFA). Sealed hermetic storage may present a practical strategy to help mitigate FFA accumulation and improve bean quality. Finally, soils exhibited sub-optimal exchangeable Ca:Mg:K ratios, with widespread K deficiency and nutrient depletion, underscoring the need for targeted nutrient replenishment. This study provides the first nationwide baseline of soil and bean Cd status, as well as key cocoa attributes of market concern in PNG, offering insights relevant to cocoa-producing regions globally.

title: 13.Climatic fingerprint of the 2023 wheat head blast outbreak and its historical and future analogs in southern South America.
abstract: Wheat head blast is a major threat to wheat in South America, but outbreaks vary across space and time because they depend on seasonal weather. In subtropical and temperate regions, epidemics occur only when winter conditions allow inoculum survival and weather during heading favors infection. As a result, epidemiological data from these regions remain limited. In 2023, unusual weather led to widespread disease occurrence across parts of southern South America. In this study, we adopted a climate-analog framework to define the climatic fingerprint of the 2023 epidemic season and assess whether similar conditions occurred historically (1981-2023) or reoccur under mid-century climate projections (2024-2055). Two biologically informed indices were developed for each year: winter thermal favorability, representing conditions for inoculum carryover, and hygrothermal suitability during heading. Historical years were compared with 2023 conditions at each site and with the 2023 Passo Fundo epidemic. Analog years were rare in the historical record, confirming the exceptional nature of 2023. Under RCP 8.5, analog frequency increased markedly in southern Brazil, indicating a higher likelihood of permissive seasons. Argentine sites became more favorable relative to their history but remained far from the Passo Fundo benchmark, whereas Artigas-Salto became less permissive due to colder winters. Overall, the 2023 climatic envelope appears historically anomalous but likely to become more frequent in southern Brazil, reinforcing the need for continued surveillance and blast-resistant management.

title: 14.Agricultural evidence synthesis at a critical juncture: quality assessment and pathways to maturation.
abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have become essential tools for synthesizing evidence to address complex agricultural challenges, yet their methodological quality remains largely uncharacterized. This study conducted a quality assessment of agricultural evidence syntheses published between 1997 and 2023. A random sample of 244 systematic reviews and meta-analyses was drawn from a bibliometric dataset of 1,709 articles. Reporting quality was evaluated using a 12-indicator rubric across four domains: reproducibility, dual-purpose infrastructure, bias mitigation, and best practices. Quality patterns were analyzed by article type and temporal trends. Predictors of reporting quality were identified through multivariate regression. Articles achieved only 32% of the maximum quality score, with major quality gaps in dual screening (4%), study quality assessment (18%), and protocol registration (12%). Systematic reviews significantly outperformed meta-analyses (6.53 vs. 3.75), suggesting divergent methodological cultures. Journal prestige and international collaboration were not associated with quality. While quality improved from 2009 to 2016, key quality indicators plateaued thereafter despite rapid publication growth. Guideline adherence emerged as the strongest quality predictor: standard guideline users scored five points higher than non-users, explaining 20% of observed variance. These findings indicate that agricultural evidence synthesis is in mid-maturation, with systemic gaps stemming from remediable knowledge and resource constraints rather than structural barriers. The strong association between guideline adherence and quality, alongside its sharp adoption increase, highlights a clear pathway for accelerating progress. To support this advancement, the CREDIT framework is proposed, targeting six interrelated needs: Collaboration, Resources, Education, Documentation, Integration, and Tools.

title: 15.Production of bottle fermented sparkling wine using nano and micro filters.
abstract: This study presents a method for the production of sparkling wine in a bottle using micro and nano- filters. The nano filter is employed for the separation of carbon dioxide from volatile aromas present in gaseous fermentation products. Nanofilters are able to pass small carbon dioxide molecules through them, which are contained in the fermentation gas. At the same time, nanofilters prevent the exit of large aromatic molecules. This process allows the wine to retain the full flavour potential of the grapes, which may be partially lost during the winemaking process. Microfilters are used to separate the majority of the wine from yeast cells, significantly simplifying the process of yeast removal from bottles after fermentation has been completed. This process is analogous to the method of removing tea leaves from a prepared infusion using a tea bag. The use of a microfilter allows for the interruption of the fermentation process at any point when the desired level of residual sugar has been reached. Various options for producing sparkling wines using the proposed method are being considered. The main focus is on the process of producing sparkling wine from wort in one stage and in one bottle. The proposed method does not require the use of expensive equipment, which makes it affordable for small-scale production and even for use at home.

title: 16.Prevalence and spatial distribution of Fusarium wilt of banana in the Peruvian Amazon.
abstract: Fusariumwilt of banana (FWB), caused byFusarium oxysporumf. sp. cubense (Foc), is a primary threat toMusaspp. production. Despite its impact, the intensity and potential drivers of the disease in the Peruvian Amazon remain poorly understood. This study assessed FWB prevalence, spatial distribution, and associated biophysical and management variables at the mesoscale. A census of 189 plots (213,005 mats) was conducted across six regions using visual inspection. Overall prevalence was 28.04%, with the highest value in Junín (55.56%). FWB was significantly associated with Isla (Iholena, AAB) and Seda (Gros Michel, AAA) cultivars. Spatial analysis revealed hierarchical aggregation with localized foci (radius = 13.8 km) and broader farm clustering at intermediate scales. Disease occurrence was more frequent in areas with higher altitudes (> 762.5 m a.s.l.) and annual precipitation (> 1481 mm). Areas with higher flood risk, linked to pronounced rainfall seasonality, were identified as critical for pathogen movement via watercourses. FWB was identified as the main phytosanitary issue in affected areas, where the lack of intervention on symptomatic plants strongly correlated with disease presence. These findings provide an epidemiological baseline for designing context-specific management and preventive strategies in the Peruvian rainforest, particularly against the emerging threat of Foc TR4, yet no present un this region of the country.

title: 17.Biomass dilution by SiO2: a reason for misinterpretation of the plant nutritional status in silicon trials.
abstract: Plants can take up significant amounts of silicon (Si), which is deposited in the apoplast as silica (SiO2). Changes in biomass and element concentrations after Si application often have been attributed to direct effects of Si on photosynthesis and nutrient uptake, not accounting for the significant biomass effect of SiO2which dilutes biomass and element concentrations. Here, we quantified this biomass dilution by SiO2and its effect on the interpretation of element concentrations. Five independent hydroponic experiments with rice, wheat, and rapeseed were conducted at different Si supply levels (0-2000 µmol L-1). Biomass and element concentrations were determined (measured data) and mathematically corrected for the SiO2content of the biomass (corrected data). With increasing Si supply, measured carbon concentrations were significantly reduced by up to 6%. This effect disappeared after mathematical correction of the SiO2dilution. Similar results were found for elements with predominantly transporter-mediated uptake. For sodium, an element taken up via bypass flow, relative concentration changes attributable to mere biomass dilution were strongly outweighed by other effects. This shows that SiO2deposition mechanistically alters the uptake processes of this element. These results illustrate that meaningful analysis of changes in nutrient uptake patterns due to Si can only be done after accounting for SiO2dilution. Not correcting the concentrations of elements by SiO2 dilution can lead to a misinterpretation of the nutritional status of plants.

title: 18.Research on rural household livelihood differentiation based on PCA and K-means algorithms: a case study of Daxing Village, Shenyang, China.
abstract: Against the backdrop of urban-rural integration and population aging, objectively quantifying the characteristics of rural household livelihood differentiation holds important reference value for understanding micro-level structural changes in rural society. Based on questionnaire survey data from 493 households in Daxing Village, Shenyang, this study constructs a livelihood indicator system comprising 14 variables across four capital dimensions. Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is employed to examine the distributional characteristics of per capita income. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) combined with K-means clustering is applied for quantitative household classification. To mitigate the interference of redundant feature information on Euclidean distance metrics, a joint parameter optimization procedure incorporating the silhouette coefficient was implemented to simultaneously select the optimal number of principal components and the number of clusters. The results indicate that: (1) the per capita income of sampled households exhibits a non-normal bimodal distribution; (2) the optimal model structure is achieved when two principal components are retained and households are partitioned into two clusters (silhouette coefficient = 0.558); and (3) sampled households are classified into "Young and Middle-aged Laborers," primarily engaged in non-agricultural employment, and "Elderly Transfer-dependent" households, who rely predominantly on policy-based transfer income. These findings suggest that the key drivers of suburban rural livelihoods are shifting from land endowments toward human capital, and that elderly households exhibit pronounced passivity in their livelihood strategies. This study provides an empirical reference for the quantitative analysis of multi-dimensional micro-level livelihood survey data.

title: 19.Laser-assisted foliar zinc delivery in grapevine: a proof-of-concept evaluation of FLB technology with conventional spray, laser-assisted spray, and laser-assisted patch delivery modes.
abstract: Zinc (Zn) deficiency is a widespread limitation in grapevine (Vitis viniferaL.) production, affecting photosynthesis, berry development, and vine health. Foliar Zn applications are constrained by the hydrophobic leaf cuticle, which restricts ionic uptake. Foliar Laser Boost (FLB) is a patented technology (US Patent 12,532,814 B2) that applies a pulsed 450 nm semiconductor diode laser to the leaf surface immediately prior to nutrient delivery, creating transient micro-apertures in the epicuticular wax layer to enhance localized foliar uptake. This proof-of-concept (PoC) study evaluated FLB-assisted zinc sulfate (ZnSO4) delivery in grapevine across four treatments: (GV UTC) untreated control; (GV S) conventional spray without laser pre-treatment; (GV LS) FLB laser pre-treatment followed by liquid spray; and (GV LP) FLB laser pre-treatment followed by biodegradable patch delivery. Leaf tissue was sampled 72 hours after treatment (T72) and analyzed by ICP-OES at Waypoint Analytical Tennessee, Inc. The untreated control yielded a baseline Zn of 49 ppm. Conventional spray without laser (GV S) raised tissue Zn to 138 ppm (+182% above UTC). FLB laser-assisted spray (GV LS) achieved 152 ppm (+210% above UTC; +10% above GV S), indicating a modest additional uplift from laser pre-treatment. FLB laser-assisted patch delivery (GV LP) produced the highest tissue Zn at 275 ppm (+461% above UTC; +99% above GV S; +81% above GV LS), demonstrating that sustained contact between the nutrient source and the laser-permeabilized cuticle substantially amplifies uptake efficiency. These preliminary results support FLB technology as a promising approach for precision foliar Zn delivery in grapevine, with the patch delivery mode showing particular efficacy. Formal statistical analysis was not possible due to the single-composite-per treatment design; replicated trials are warranted.

title: 20.A revised method for estimating breeding population size in native equine breeds: scientific rationale, genetic implications, and policy relevance.
abstract: Background: Reliable estimates of breeding population size are critical for conservation of rare livestock breeds. Traditional methods in the UK have used recent pedigree registrations multiplied by species specific factors to estimate breeding females. However, equine breeds show highly variable and sporadic breeding patterns, rendering multiplier-based approaches unsuitable. Many mares produce only one or two foals in a lifetime and numerous equines never enter breeding programs. Additionally, incomplete reporting of deaths inflates counts of potential breeders. These issues complicate the identification of at risk native pony and horse breeds and the allocation of conservation resources. Methods: The UK Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra), in collaboration with the UK Genetics for Livestock and Equines Committee (UKGLE), developed a 10-year retrospective quantification method, often referred to as amultiplier, to directly enumerate breeding females. Under this new method, a mare is counted as part of the breeding population if she has produced at least one registered foal in the past 10 years and is still alive at the end of that period. Each qualifying mare is included starting from the year she first foals and for ten years after her last foaling, unless recorded deceased. Mares with no offspring are excluded as they made no genetic contribution. We review prior approaches, detail the rationale behind the 10-year multiplier (including a conceptual diagram, Figure 1), and interpret this method in light of population genetics theory (effective population sizeNe, inbreeding coefficientsF, mean kinshipMK). We compare the new approach to international practices (FAO, Rare Breeds Survival Trust) and discuss its implications for conservation policy. Results: The 10-year breeding female multiplier provides a more accurate and breed-specific estimate of active broodmare numbers compared to earlier proxy measures. It inherently adjusts for the longer generational interval of equines (~8-10 years) and irregular foaling schedules. By focusing on mares that reproduced, it avoids overestimating genetic contributors such as by counting all mature females and underestimating long-interval breeders which a short-term metric could exclude. Preliminary application indicates that for some breeds, the new method yields significantly different (often lower) breeding population estimates than prior speculative multipliers, aligning better with known studbook trends. The method outputs also enable direct calculation ofNeusing the true number of breeding males and females, rather than cruder assumptions. For example, using the new data, the averageNeof UK native horse breeds was ~100 in 2019-2024 (down from ~224 in 2000), and several breeds (e.g. four horse breeds in 2024) show critically lowNe≤ 50. This underscores the urgency of effective breeding management. Integrating pedigree analyses, breed societies have begun monitoring mean inbreeding and kinship of the counted breeding population, as advocated by conservation geneticists. The Rare Breeds Survival Trust's recent watchlist methodology shift toNeand inbreeding metrics complements this 10-year multiplier, yielding a more holistic risk assessment. Internationally, the UK's approach exemplifies a move from simple numeric thresholds towards demographic-genetic indicators in breed conservation. Conclusions: The newly implemented 10-year multiplier for quantifying the population of breeding mares provides a scientifically robust and transparent means to estimate the genetic breeding population of equine breeds. It directly addresses biological realities of equine reproduction and resolves the shortcomings of prior indirect estimation. Coupling this demographic metric with genetic diversity measures (effective size, inbreeding rate, MK) offers a powerful tool for conservation decision-making. This approach ensures that at-risk status and related policy support (e.g. inclusion on the Native Breeds at Risk list) are grounded in meaningful data on both population size and genetic health. The method has broad implications: it can improve the accuracy of national and international breed risk registries, guide targeted interventions (such as breeding programs or incentives to utilize underrepresented mares), and ultimately enhance the long-term viability of the UK's native horse and pony breeds.

title: 21.Impact of grape seed extract on flavor and functionality of pea protein extrudates and patties.
abstract: Consumer interest in plant-based proteins is increasing, but undesirable off-flavors from Maillard reaction and lipid oxidation processes hinder their broader acceptance. Our previous work showed that proanthocyanidin-rich plant extracts like grape seed extract (GSE) could reduce formation of these off-flavors in aqueous plant protein solutions. This study investigated the effects of GSE addition pre- and post-extrusion at two levels (0.02 and 1.0% w/w) on off-flavor development in pea protein extrudates and patties. We hypothesized that GSE addition at different processing phases would impact its ability to alter Maillard reaction and lipid oxidation processes, thus affecting its ability to mitigate off-flavor formation. Pre-extrusion treatments reduced Maillard browning products by 40% more than post-extrusion treatments, likely because GSE polyphenols were present throughout extrusion-induced protein denaturation and restructuring, which allowed them to bind reactive amino groups and limit amino acid interaction with reducing sugars. Conversely, post-extrusion GSE treatment decreased primary and secondary lipid oxidation products by approximately 53% and 44% in patties, respectively (vs 15% and 31%, respectively, in pre-treated samples), and enhanced antioxidant capacities across all samples. Because post-extrusion GSE treatments exhibited fewer protein-polyphenol interactions, polyphenols were able to scavenge free radicals more efficiently than pre-extrusion treatments. Sensory evaluation indicated that GSE did not impart astringency, a common concern with polyphenol addition. These results demonstrate that polyphenols can effectively improve flavor quality in plant-based protein products. Practical Application: Addition of grape seed extract can help reduce off-flavors in legumes caused by major flavor degradation pathways. In particular, adding polyphenols before processing can reduce Maillard-derived off-flavors, while polyphenols added after processing are more effective at reducing lipid oxidation-derived off-flavors. This approach offers a simple and sustainable way to enhance flavor quality and properties of plant-based meat alternatives.

title: 22.Laser-assisted foliar phosphorus delivery in strawberry: comparing low-dose FLB applications against conventional high-volume spray.
abstract: Conventional high-volume foliar sprays deliver large quantities of nutrients per application but risk phytotoxicity and waste active ingredients. Foliar Laser Boost (FLB) technology employs a handheld pulsed laser to create transient micro-perforations in the leaf cuticle, enabling highly localized nutrient delivery at substantially reduced doses. This randomized controlled trial evaluated FLB-assisted phosphorus (P) delivery in strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa cv. Chandler) under greenhouse conditions (Chula, GA, 2026). Sixty plants were assigned to five treatments (12 replicates each): (T1) untreated control; (T2) high-volume conventional micro-spray (10 mL of 0-0-26 solution per whole plant; ~2,840 mg P); (T3) low-dose micro-spray (0.2 mL applied to one leaf; ~77 mg P); (T4) FLB micro-spray (laser pre-treatment followed by 0.2 mL on one leaf); and (T5) FLB patch (laser pre-treatment followed by 0.2 mL delivered via biodegradable patch). Leaf tissue P content (% dry weight), chlorophyll content (mg/cm2, AtLeaf CHL Plus), and phytotoxicity (% necrosis) were assessed at 3 and 7 days after treatment (DAT). T2 caused severe phytotoxicity (45% at 3 DAT; 70.4% at 7 DAT; F = 1,056.7, p < 0.0001) due to undiluted solution application, and achieved the highest P uptake (2.44% at 3 DAT; 2.02% at 7 DAT). FLB-assisted treatments (T4: 0.80%; T5: 0.74% at 3 DAT) exceeded the low-dose control without laser (T3: 0.66%); at 7 DAT, T4 and T3 retained similar P levels (0.44% vs. 0.43%), while T5 declined toward the baseline (0.36%). FLB treatments achieved meaningful P enrichment using ~37-fold less product than the conventional spray, with minimal phytotoxicity (0-0.8%). These results demonstrate that FLB technology enables substantial input reduction without proportional loss of foliar nutrient uptake efficacy, supporting its viability as a precision delivery platform.

title: 23.Protecting wild populations and working landscapes: the case for transitioning to size-based criteria for federal regulation of American ginseng.
abstract: Overharvesting of wild medicinal plants threatens biodiversity, rural livelihoods, and the long-term sustainability of harvested populations worldwide. Wild American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius L.) is listed on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and, as a result, is regulated in the United States under a federally coordinated, age-based harvest framework intended to sustain natural populations. However, age-based criteria assume strong, consistent relationships between plant age, size, and reproductive capacity—relationships that do not hold up for many other plant and animal species, and have been questioned for American ginseng. We test whether size-based metrics provide a stronger and more practical basis for regulating ginseng harvest than chronological age. We measured age, aboveground traits, root biomass, and reproductive output for wild-simulated ginseng plants (5–10 years old) across four sites spanning substantial environmental heterogeneity. Leaf area, estimated from a simple field measurement, explained 75% of the variation in root dry mass, far exceeding the explanatory power of age (12%) or the combination of age and leaf count (36%), representing the current regulatory approach. Leaf area also strongly predicted the probability of reproduction and maximum seed production, with larger plants consistently outperforming smaller, older individuals. Our results demonstrate that age-based harvest criteria are weak proxies for the biological attributes most relevant to conservation and sustainability. A simple, field-measurable size metric better reflects ginseng performance and could underpin a transition to size-based regulation, analogous to widely used approaches in fisheries management.

title: 24.Automated high-throughput hyperspectral imaging enables earlydetection of grapevine downy mildew and monitoring of vineyard spray program performance.
abstract: Grapevine downy mildew (GDM), caused byPlasmopara viticola, is managed largely through repeated fungicide applications, yet evaluating spray-program performance is difficult because field infections are spatially heterogeneous. However, host physiological changes can precede visible symptom development. We tested whether standardized, high-throughput VNIR hyperspectral imaging of field-grown grapevine leaf discs can capture early optical changes associated with infection and discriminate program-linked mitigation. Leaves were collected from a 2025 vineyard trial in Geneva, NY (cv. La Crescent) managed under three spray programs (conventional fungicides, biofungicides, and untreated control). Leaf discs (≈87 per program) were excised, inoculated withP. viticola, and imaged at 0.5, 1.5, and 3.5 days post inoculation (dpi) using a custom built, automated, hyperspectral imaging microscopy platform (400-980 nm). No visible sporulation occurred at 0.5 or 1.5 dpi; sporulation was first observed at 3.5 dpi and occurred only in the untreated control, whereas no discs from either treated program sporulated. Multivariate spectral analyses showed significant separation by spray program and dpi, and disease-related spectral indices exhibited program-dependent trajectories, with treated discs showing attenuated optical change relative to the control. A random-forest classifier trained on pre-sporulation spectra (0.5 and 1.5 dpi; N = 169) predicted subsequent sporulation with 0.78 accuracy and 0.77 ROC-AUC (95% CI 0.70-0.85), highlighting informative bands across visible, red-edge, and near-infrared regions. Together, these results support outcome-linked, replicate-rich hyperspectral phenotyping of vineyard spray programs using field-derived material under standardized acquisition conditions.

title: 25.Toward causal designs to quantify management-driven soil carbon change at multi-field scales.
abstract: Agricultural policies for climate mitigation and adaptation depend on sustainable management of soil carbon. Controlled field experiments demonstrate that regenerative practices increase soil carbon, yet expected changes are often small relative to spatial and sampling variation. This variation may hinder the ability to quantify management impacts at the scale of working landscapes. Here, we test this expectation using temporal data on surface soil carbon concentrations. We evaluate a quasi-experimental design to estimate change in concentrations under distinct management regimes in an agricultural growing region located in the Hudson Valley, NY. We stratified eligible fields representing regional agricultural practices by initial soil organic carbon (SOC) and soil texture and selected 80 fields within these strata to enable comparisons among management regimes. We sampled each field at an average density of 0.6 hectares per soil core in the non-growing seasons of 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 (796 sampling points; 1592 samples). We evaluated spatial and temporal variability in soil carbon and how these sources of variation influence detectability of management effects. Spatial variability in soil carbon was large both within and among fields. However, repeated sampling of fixed-point locations reduced between-field variability in soil carbon change, improving detectability of management effects despite high spatial heterogeneity. Minimum detectable differences were smaller than expected soil carbon responses over management-relevant time horizons (e.g., 5-10 years). Estimated management effects depended on the representativeness of sampled fields, with non-representative sampling across soil texture altering the estimated treatment effect. Our results suggest that causal, field-scale studies based on remeasurement of fixed points and appropriate comparison groups can detect and quantify management effects under real-world agricultural conditions. Such studies at the scale of commercial agriculture are needed to build confidence about when, where, and which regenerative practices deliver benefits such as improved soil health, informing policies for more sustainable and climate-smart agriculture.

title: 26.A four-layer framework for independent credibility assessment of sensor-derived livestock data: development and demonstration on dairy cattle accelerometer and automatic feed bin datasets.
abstract: Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) sensor systems generate continuous, high-resolution data increasingly used in farm management, welfare certification, sustainability reporting, and agricultural finance. However, the preprocessing pipelines that transform raw sensor output into analysis-ready datasets and alarm systems are typically undocumented and unstandardised, limiting the ability of downstream users to assess data credibility. This paper reports the development and demonstration of a four-layer framework for independent credibility assessment of PLF sensor data, comprising: 1. structural integrity validation; 2. biological plausibility scoring against published reference ranges; 3. temporal consistency analysis; and 4. quantified Farm Reliability Score (0-100) with a 95% Wilson confidence interval. The framework was implemented in R and applied to two synthetic datasets generated to reflect the statistical properties of commercial and research dairy cattle sensor data, preserving realistic flag rates and variable distributions while containing no real animal records: an activity monitoring accelerometer dataset (n=41 animals, 63 days) and an automatic feed bin system dataset (n=38 animals, 45 days). The accelerometer dataset received a Farm Reliability Score of 87.3 (Good; 95% CI: 83.1-91.2), with biological plausibility flags as the primary penalty contributor and a novel transition directionality mismatch detected in 1.6% of interval records. The feed bin dataset received a score of 91.8 (Excellent; 95% CI: 88.4-95.2). The framework architecture is sensor- and animal species agnostic and extensible to additional PLF technology categories. Results demonstrate that structured, multi layer validation detects data quality issues invisible to completeness checks alone, and that the scoring approach produces outputs interpretable by both technical and non-technical stakeholders. The framework's relevance to institutional data use contexts, limitations, and the research required to establish cross-platform threshold standards are discussed.

title: 27.Mathematical modeling of honey bee population dynamics using complex variables: balancing breed conservation and genetic diversity with inbreeding.
abstract: The global decline of honey bee (Apis mellifera) populations poses a significant threat to biodiversity and food security. A key challenge lies in balancing the conservation of local breeds with maintaining population genetic health. We propose an innovative spatially explicit model based on complex-variable theory, where the state of a population is described by a complex variable z ε C (with Re(z) representing productivity and Im(z) representing adaptability). The model introduces the concept of "population quality" (Q)-a standardized metric synthesizing a colony's (population's) productive potential and adaptive capacity, adjusted for environmental factors (population fluctuations) and genetic processes (drift, mutation, selection, migration). The framework incorporates a modified Ginzburg-Landau equation with dynamics for the inbreeding coefficient (F). Numerical simulations were performed on a 100×100 grid using a semi-implicit integration scheme. A systematic exploration of the parameter space revealed critical ranges: migrationD=0.03±0.01 and competitiong=2.8±0.2, which yield a stable balance between pure breed preservation (25-30%) and maintenance of genetic diversity (4-6% hybrids). A strong negative correlation was found between inbreeding and population quality (r=-0.89±0.04,p< 0.001), with a critical threshold ofFcrit=0.07. The negative effects of inbreeding became statistically significant 3-4.5 years after the onset of population isolation. The model was validated against monitoring data from populations in the South Altai region. The proposed model provides a quantitative foundation for developing strategies to preserve bee genetic diversity. The identified parameters and timeframes enable optimized population management, helping to prevent inbreeding depression while sustaining breed diversity.

title: 28.Enhanced foliar delivery of oxytetracycline in citrus through laser-assisted cuticle modification: a proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Foliar application of agricultural inputs faces significant barriers due to the leaf cuticle, which limits penetration and uptake of active compounds. This study evaluates the Foliar Laser Boost (FLB) technology, which employs selective laser ablation to create microscopic channels in the leaf cuticle, potentially enhancing the delivery of foliar-applied compounds. We conducted a proof-of-concept experiment using oxytetracycline hydrochloride (OTC) as a model compound on thornless key lime (Citrus aurantiifolia) shrubs. Three treatments were compared: untreated control, conventional micro-sprayer application, and FLB treatment followed by localized micro sprayer application. Leaf tissue samples were analyzed 48 hours post-application using LC MS/MS. Results showed dramatic differences in OTC concentrations: control (31.4 ppb), conventional spray (931.4 ppb), and FLB + micro-spray (18,900.4 ppb). The FLB treatment demonstrated approximately 20-fold higher OTC uptake compared to conventional application and 602-fold higher than the untreated control. These findings provide strong preliminary evidence that laser-assisted cuticle modification can significantly enhance foliar delivery efficiency, with potential applications in precision agriculture for improved pesticide, nutrient, and biological agent delivery.

title: 29.Soil silicon application alleviates drought stress in sugar beet (Beta vulgaris L.) in Central Europe.
abstract: Background: The increasing frequency and intensity of drought events has led to yield and quality losses in sugar beet production in temperate regions in Central Europe. Under arid conditions, silicon (Si) application reduced beet yield losses under drought. Similar data for temperate climates are missing. Moreover, most studies focused either on foliar application or drip irrigation with Si. Aims: The aim of this study was to determine the effect of soil Si application on yield and quality parameters ofBeta vulgarisin a temperate environment. Methods: Field trials were conducted at three different sites in Germany and Austria. Different Si fertilization rates were tested (site 1: 0, 37, 78 kg ha-1; site 2 and 3: 0, 50 kg ha-1). At site 1, an irrigated control and a non-irrigated drought treatment were established. At sites 2 and 3, irrigation was not possible. Yield and quality parameters were determined after harvest. Results: At site 1, drought stress reduced beet yield by 30% without Si application. Under drought conditions, Si led to a significant reduction of beet yield and net sugar yield losses by 17 and 18%, respectively. Quality parameters were only affected by irrigation, not by Si. No natural drought stress occurred at sites 2 and 3. Conclusions: The results indicate that Si fertilization could become a relevant tool for sugar beet cultivation in a changing climate. The mechanisms behind this yield effect are yet to be determined. More data is needed to propose clear Si fertilizer recommendations for sugar beet cultivation in Central Europe.

title: 30.The energy return on energy investment of dairy-bred beef production in Ireland.
abstract: Food production - including beef production - in the industrialised world relies heavily on fossil fuels. At the same time, IPCC mitigation pathways consistent with keeping global warming below 2°C indicate reductions of around 70%-90% in fossil fuel use by 2050. In Ireland, the trend in agriculture is consolidating on intensive dairy production. Male progeny from the national dairy herd are a low-value, co-product usually sold to beef farms for finishing. This study examined the Energy Return on Energy Invested (EROI) of a beef finishing farm in Ireland to determine its long-term viability. Farm energy inputs were determined and set against the total beef energy output. Energy inputs include diesel, electricity, embodied energy of fertiliser, buildings, machinery and other infrastructure necessary to produce beef on the farm. Energy output was defined as the calorific content of all beef produced on the farm in a year. Energy input totalled 1,131 GJ and the energy output totalled 300 GJ, giving an EROI of 0.27:1. When only recurring energy inputs are considered, the EROI of the farm is 0.48:1. Compared to other beef EROI studies, this is towards the upper end of reported beef EROI values. However, like other food production systems, beef production is heavily dependent on non-renewable inputs, with the renewable share of inputs at just 2.10%.

title: 31.Efficacy of selected insecticides against the two-spot cotton leafhopper Amrasca biguttula (Ishida) on Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, 2026.
abstract: The two-spot cotton leafhopper (TSCL),Amrasca biguttula, is an emerging invasive pest of ornamental crops in the southeastern United States, where feeding by adults and nymphs causes hopperburn and reduces plant quality and marketability. This study provides the first U.S. field evaluation of insecticides for managing TSCL on hibiscus, assessing the efficacy and residual performance of several IRAC groups under field nursery conditions. Hibiscus plants (H. rosa-sinensis'Hot Shot') of uniform size and age were obtained from a commercial nursery on 22 August 2025 and planted into 5-gallon pots containing a commercial substrate. Plants were maintained outdoors on a nursery pad at the Clemson University Pee Dee Research and Education Center (Florence County, SC). Plants were placed under protective netted tents to reduce interference from natural enemies and rainfall while remaining fully exposed to ambient temperature [average ≈ 82°F (28°C)], humidity (average = ≈ 75%), wind, and sunlight. TSCL infestations were established by placing infested cotton branches onto hibiscus plants weekly for two months. All flower buds and older leaves were removed to promote vegetative growth. Plants were irrigated on an alternate-day schedule and received one liquid fertilizer application during the season. Treatments were arranged in a randomized complete block design with six replicates, and each replicate consisted of three leaves sampled from the top, middle, and bottom canopy positions. Adult and nymph counts were recorded independently at the top, middle, and bottom canopy positions. Positional values were kept separate during data entry. Foliar sprays were applied to wet foliage using a CO₂-pressurized backpack sprayer operated at 30 psi and equipped with a TeeJet XR 8002VS flat-fan nozzle. The first application was made on 13 Oct 2025. After the first application, conditions were: ambient temperature 78°F (25.5°C), relative humidity 74%, soil temperature (1.6 in) 91°F (32.5°C), canopy temperature 87°F (30.7°C), and wind 7 mph from the north. Treatment pots were positioned apart from untreated pots to reduce spray drift. The second application was made on 10 Nov 2025, exactly 28 days after the first application. After the second application, conditions were: ambient temperature 52°F (11.1°C), relative humidity 41%, soil temperature (1.6 in) 54°F (12.2°C), canopy temperature 52°F (11.0°C), and wind 12 mph from the west. Adults and nymphs were counted visually using a hand lens before treatment and again at 7, 14, 21, 28, and 35 days after the first treatment (DAT). Data at each post-treatment sample date were analyzed using one-way ANOVA. When significant treatment effects were detected (P < 0.05), treatment means were separated using Fisher's LSD test, and values are presented as means ± standard error. Before the first treatment, adult and nymph densities did not differ among treatments (Tables 1-2). At 7 DAT, significant differences were detected for both adults and nymphs. Adult counts were lowest in Hachi Hachi, followed in order of suppression by Talstar, Altus, Safari, Ventigra, and Mainspring, all of which differed from the nontreated control (Table 1). Nymph suppression was strongest in Hachi Hachi, followed by Talstar, Altus, Safari, and Ventigra, while Mainspring provided weaker nymph suppression (Table 2). At 14 DAT, treatment differences remained significant. Hachi Hachi and Altus maintained the lowest adult densities, and Hachi Hachi and Safari maintained the lowest nymph densities, while Mainspring showed a rebound in both life stages. Safari, Ventigra, and Talstar continued to provide consistent suppression (Tables 1 and 2). At 21 and 28 DAT, representing the extended residual period following the first spray, significant treatment differences persisted. Hachi Hachi, Altus, Safari, Ventigra, and Talstar maintained low adult and nymph densities through 28 DAT. Mainspring exhibited limited residual activity, with higher counts than other treated plants. The nontreated control consistently had the highest densities. At 21 and 28 DAT, representing the extended residual period following the first spray, significant treatment differences persisted. Hachi-Hachi SC and Safari maintained the lowest adult and nymph densities at both time points, while Altus and Ventigra also provided sustained suppression but at slightly higher levels. Talstar maintained moderate suppression, with adult and nymph densities higher than the strongest treatments at 21 DAT, but improved performance by 28 DAT. Mainspring exhibited limited residual activity, with consistently higher densities than other treated plants. The nontreated control had the highest densities throughout. A two-spray program spaced 28 days apart maintained suppression for six weeks, aligning with the final month and a half before plants flower and are prepared for shipping and sale. Maintaining low TSCL populations during the pre-shipping period is important due to regulatory concerns and spread risk, and we used a 28-day reapplication interval because it reflects common nursery practice and reduces labor and application frequency.

title: 32.Studies of the leaf and leaf stalk anatomy and taxonomy of the trichomes in some species of Cucurbitaceae L. in Iraq.
abstract: When establishing and describing different levels of classification, such as family, genus, species, or taxonomy, anatomical studies are a crucial taxonomic guide. In this study, cross sections were taken of leaf petioles, leaf blades, midribs, and epidermal trichome. According to the results, the shape of epidermal cells, the thickness and quantity of spongy and sclerenchyma tissue layers, the shape of the petiole, the thickness of the chlorenchyma layer, the collenchyma, the thickness and quantity of vascular bundles, and the shape of the outer blastula were all markedly different. We also observed different types of epidermal trichome in the studied plant species. This study has added to the body of knowledge about trichomes types and the anatomy of the petiole and leaf blade in six different plant species from the Cucurbitaceae family. The study aims to investigate the leaf and petiole anatomy and the taxonomic characteristics of trichomes in selected species of the familyCucurbitaceaein Iraq, in order to identify diagnostic features useful for species differentiation, clarify their taxonomic relationships, and enhance the understanding of their systematic classification within the family.

title: 33.Foundation model-assisted segmentation enables robust field-based severity estimation: a case-study of coffee leaf rust.
abstract: Accurate estimation of coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix) severity remains challenging due to symptom heterogeneity, illumination variability, and observer subjectivity, particularly under field conditions. We developed a segmentation pipeline combining zero-shot foundational models (SAM3) and fine-tuned deep learning (SAM2) for percent severity estimation, and compared them with three other segmentation approaches: DeepLabV3+ (convolutional neural network model), ImageJ (color thresholding), and pliman R package (palette-based). A total of 1,285 images were collected across several field plots, and 606 pixel-level rust lesion masks were curated for model fine-tuning and independent evaluation. A two-stage detection-segmentation workflow integrating YOLOv8 and SAM2 enabled robust leaf extraction from complex branch-level images, with detection performance consistently exceeding 0.98 across metrics. For lesion segmentation, at the pixel level, the zero-shot foundation model SAM3 achieved the highest disease segmentation performance (median Dice ≈ 0.91; IoU ≈ 0.83), with balanced precision (≈ 0.93) and recall (≈ 0.94). DeepLabV3+ also performed well (Dice ≈ 0.86; IoU ≈ 0.75), whereas classical threshold-based approaches showed high recall but substantially lower precision, indicating frequent false positives and producing a systematic positive bias. SAM2 exhibited more conservative performance, yielding higher precision but reduced recall relative to SAM3. At the leaf level, the highest agreement between predicted and reference severity estimates were found for SAM3, followed by DeepLabV3+ and SAM2, while classical methods overestimated diseased area. Overall, SAM3 led to a more robust, scalable, and consistent severity estimation under real-world field conditions.

title: 34.Isolation, characterization, and classification of soils along the toposequence in Kersa sub-watershed, eastern Ethiopia.
abstract: Soil classification is an important tool for identifying the most appropriate use of soils as well as for sustainable utilization of the scarce soil resource. This study was undertaken in Kersa sub-watershed of East Hararghe zone, Oromia region, Ethiopia, to investigate the site morphological, selected physical and chemical characteristics, and classify soils. Eight representative pedons were opened at three topographic positions (upper, middle, and lower) and described in the field. Disturbed and undisturbed soil samples from identifiable genetic horizons were taken for laboratory analysis of physical and chemical properties. Soils varied considerably across the topographic positions and soil depth in terms of their morphological, physical, and chemical attributes. Soil depth ranged from very shallow (25 cm) in the upper topographic positions to very deep (200 cm) in the lower topographic positions. Surface soil texture varied from sandy loam to clay loam, while subsurface textures ranged from sandy loam to clay. Bulk density ranged from 1.10 to 1.42 g/cm3and increased with depth in all pedons. Soil pH (H2O) ranged from moderately alkaline (7.50) to slightly acid (6.27), with higher values recorded in lower topographic positions. Organic carbon content was low to very low (0.56-1.87%) and decreased with depth in all pedons. Cation exchange capacity ranged from 21.3 to 43.2 cmol(+) kg-1, with the highest values in lower topographic positions. Base saturation was high (>80%) in all pedons. Following the field survey and soil analytical results, five reference soil groups were identified following the World Reference Base (WRB) legend: Gleyic Vertic Luvisols (Clayic, Cutanic) and Haplic Vertisols (Mollic) in the lower topographic position; Hypereutric Cambisols (Loamic) in the middle topographic position; and Hypereutric Leptosols (Loamic) and Hypereutric Endoleptic Regosols (Loamic) in the upper topographic position. The results revealed the dominant role of topography in soil formation and development, and the requirement of site-specific soil management interventions in Kersa sub-watershed.

title: 35.Isolation, characterization, and phosphate solubilization efficiency of bacteria from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) rhizosphere soils in Galana District, Southern Ethiopia.
abstract: Phosphorus is an essential element for plant growth, yet its bioavailability in tropical soils is often limited due to fixation into insoluble forms. This study aimed to isolate and characterize phosphate solubilizing bacteria (PSB) from common bean (Phaseolus vulgarisL.) rhizosphere soils in Galana District, southern Ethiopia. Thirty rhizosphere soil samples were collected from six kebeles. PSB were isolated using serial dilution on Pikovskaya agar containing tricalcium phosphate. Fifty-four bacterial isolates were obtained, of which 10 strains showing the highest solubilization efficiency were selected for characterization. Solubilization index ranged from 2.29 to 3.88, with isolate GPSB04 showing the highest efficiency (3.88) followed by GPSB11 (3.44). All isolates demonstrated significant pH reduction in PVK broth from 7.01 to 3.99-6.41 after 7 days, indicating organic acid production. All isolates were Gram-negative, rod-shaped cells forming round colonies with varying colors. Biochemical tests showed 60% of isolates produced indole-3-acetic acid, while 100% produced hydrogen cyanide, ammonia, and hydrogen sulfide. All isolates grew at 10-40°C, with 20% tolerating 5-45°C. Salt tolerance ranged from 0.5-5% NaCl, and pH tolerance ranged from 4.5-8.5. Phosphate solubilization efficiency correlated strongly with pH reduction (r = -0.72). These results demonstrate that common bean rhizosphere in Galana District harbors diverse PSB with potential for biofertilizer development. Isolates GPSB04, GPSB11, and GPSB21 are recommended for further greenhouse and field evaluation.

title: 36.Standard area diagram design determines accuracy, speed, and sampling efficiency in coffee leaf rust assessment.
abstract: Although standard area diagrams (SAD) are widely used to reduce subjectivity in visual disease assessment, their design has often prioritized accuracy metrics without explicit consideration of assessment efficiency and operational feasibility. Here, we developed a simplified two-color, 10-diagram SAD to aid coffee leaf rust (CLR, caused byHemileia vastatrix) severity assessment and evaluated its performance in terms of accuracy, reliability, and implications for assessment time and field sampling efficiency. Seventeen raters provided visual estimates that were unaided, aided by an existing true-color 21-diagram SADs, and aided by the new SAD; estimates were compared against reference values obtained by manual annotation. The new SAD achieved the highest mean overall accuracy (Lin's CCC > 0.93) and bias correction coefficient (Cb = 0.97). Coverage probability (CP = 0.70) was higher than for unaided assessments (CP = 0.29) and the existing SAD (CP = 0.65). Interrater reliability was consistently high across methods (ICC > 0.90), indicating that improvements were primarily due to reduced systematic error rather than changes in rater consistency. Field evaluations confirmed that both SAD were similarly effective (CCC > 0.86). The minimum number of plants required to achieve a 95% confidence interval half-width of ±2 percentage points increased with mean field severity and depended on sampling design and SAD method, ranging from 3-8 plants in the low-severity field to >40 plants under the least intensive design in the high-severity field. Predicted total field time ranged from <10 to 50 minutes across scenarios, and the new SAD reduced assessment time by approximately 11-13% while maintaining the same precision target. Overall, a simplified SAD can preserve statistical performance while improving operational efficiency, enabling the same level of precision with reduced field effort.

title: 37.Cultivating evidence: the evolution, collaboration, and intellectual landscape of evidence synthesis research in agriculture.
abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have become essential infrastructure for translating agricultural research into actionable knowledge, yet the field's developmental trajectory and intellectual structure remain poorly characterized. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 1,709 evidence synthesis publications in agricultural sciences, examining growth dynamics, collaboration, thematic evolution, and geographic specialization. Results show exponential growth of 29% annually with a 2018 inflection point marking transition from emerging methodology to mainstream practice. Meta-analyses, comprising 75% of publications and accelerating earlier (2017) than systematic reviews (2019), have primarily driven this expansion as an accessible quantitative approach. Evidence synthesis is highly collaborative, with 59% multi-country authorship sustained across 97 countries and regions. Topic modeling identified 14 core themes spanning soil carbon, climate change, crop management, technology adoption, and sustainable agriculture, with thematic shifts from production-focused topics toward climate and sustainability priorities aligned with post-2015 policy agendas. Strategic diagram analysis revealed a linear structure linking topic maturity and centrality, indicating exceptional integration distinct from the fragmentation typical of other domains. Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) analysis showed geographic specialization aligned with national agricultural contexts, though concentration of synthesis capacity raises equity concerns about whose systems and questions are represented. Overall, agricultural evidence synthesis has matured into a globally connected, policy-responsive knowledge network, yet sustaining growth will require institutional support, methodological rigor, and pathways that translate synthesis into practice impact.

title: 38.Hybrid CNN-LSTM approach for predicting coconut maturity.
abstract: This study presents a hybrid deep learning approach for predicting the maturity of coconuts based on their images using deep learning techniques. Accurately determining coconut maturity is essential for optimizing market value and utilization. Traditional methods rely heavily on manual assessments, which are time-consuming, subjective, and prone to errors. To address this, a hybrid deep learning model combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks was developed. Using the pre-trained Xception model for feature extraction, the CNN captured spatial features, while the LSTM layers modeled temporal dependencies for classifying coconuts into three maturity stages: 6th month, 7th month, and 8th month. The model achieved a classification accuracy of 85%, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, the trained model was integrated into a user-friendly Streamlit application, enabling real-time, field based predictions for farmers. This innovation provides a reliable, efficient, and scalable solution for automating coconut maturity assessment, enhancing productivity in the agricultural sector.

title: 39.Estimating potential yield and economic losses caused by an emergent quarantine pest using farmer surveys and temperature-driven risk modeling: the case of the potato psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli) in Peru.
abstract: Emerging and quarantine pests threaten crops and food security, particularly in low-income countries, where data on past damage are scarce. In these settings, rapid estimates of potential yield and economic losses are essential for informing pest management and policy, often relying on alternative data and modeling approaches. Following the recent emergence of potato psyllids in Peru, this study developed an integrative framework to estimate potential losses. The approach combines (i) farmer-reported yield losses and management practices from 109 potato farmers in northern Peru, (ii) temperature-based modeling to identify climatically suitable areas for pest establishment, and (iii) regional potato production statistics to assess the national exposure. Approximately 37% of Peru's potato-growing areas were classified as having a high climatic risk. Integrating these areas with farmer reports yielded an estimated national loss of 18.8%, equivalent to approximately 981,000 tons, valued at USD 108 million. Surveys also revealed severe household impacts, limited effectiveness of commonly used insecticides, and greater vulnerability among female farmers in the region.

title: 40.Joint modeling of wheat head blast and water deficit risks for climate-informed sowing calendar decisions for rainfed wheat in the Brazilian Cerrado.
abstract: Wheat blast, caused byPyricularia oryzaeTriticum lineage, is a major constraint to wheat expansion in the Brazilian Cerrado. Delayed sowing is often recommended for disease avoidance; however, late sowing can increase the risk of water deficit. This study quantifies the joint risks from head blast and water deficit in the Brazilian Cerrado to inform sowing-date recommendations. Using daily weather data from a 62-year period (1961-2023), crop phenology was simulated with an accumulated growing degree day approach to estimate heading and maturity dates for six sowing dates defined at 10-day intervals across the sowing window, starting on February 25. Epidemic probability was calculated using a logistic model, while water-deficit events were identified based on an accumulated effective precipitation threshold (150 mm) during crop growth. For each pixel within the potential wheat area in the Cerrado and for each sowing date, we empirically estimated the probability of at least one hazard, fitted smooth pixel-wise probability curves, and identified the optimal sowing date. A spatially smoothed 7-day bin classification was used to generate a practical sowing-recommendation map. In addition, we assessed the effects of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation on epidemic probability. Results showed that mid- to late-March sowings generally minimize joint risk. Spatial heterogeneity highlighted regions suitable for earlier sowing and potential expansion. El Niño/La Niña events amplified/suppressed epidemic probability, particularly for intermediate sowing dates where sensitivity was greatest. These findings support region-specific, multi-hazard sowing recommendations and the incorporation of climate-variability signals into decision support for tropical rainfed wheat.

title: 41.Modelling the adoption of Integrated Pest Management: informing policy approaches to pesticide-reduction targets.
abstract: UK crop growers face challenges in maintaining yields to meet food demands whilst mitigating environmental impacts of farming.
