There is attention on policies advocating sustainable alternatives to pesticide use for the long-term control and prevention of crop diseases. One such method is Integrated Pest Management (IPM), which despite its acknowledged effectiveness, has seen limited adoption in the UK to date. The 'UK Pesticides National Action Plan 2025' sets a minimum target for reducing impacts of pesticide use, while also supporting increased uptake of IPM. We developed a joint epidemiological-behavioural model forSeptoria triticiblotch in wheat, parameterised using contemporary data. Performing simulations with the model, in which growers could choose to use either IPM, or a conventional fungicide regime, the projected rate of IPM adoption would not meet the UK's pesticide reduction targets for 2030. We found that policies addressing behavioural barriers had the greatest potential to improve these adoption trends, with lesser improvements for investment in IPM research and financial subsidies. A push for initial adoption also increased the likelihood of attaining time-dependant pesticide-reduction targets. We therefore encourage IPM adoption policies that can improve growers' knowledge and access to IPM implementation training, resources and services.

title: 42.From hand tools to mechanization: characterizing gaps and opportunities for maize, bean, and coffee smallholders in Honduras.
abstract: This study characterized agricultural mechanization and identified the main challenges and opportunities for maize, bean and coffee production systems across five departments in Honduras: Lempira, Copán, Intibucá, Olancho and El Paraíso. A total of 112 surveys were conducted, and four focus groups were held among farmers. The surveys gathered information on production systems and types of tools used, while focus groups explored perceptions of farmers about the challenges and mechanization needs. The farmers surveyed grow maize (95.5%), bean (92.9%), and coffee (38.4%), on areas smaller than 1 ha for maize and bean (73%) and from 1 to 5 ha for coffee (51.2%), located on hillsides, plains, and mixed terrain. The use of motorized tools varied greatly between sites and crops (0-65.1%), while the use of hand tools was reported by almost all respondents (90.7 95.2%). Overall, the tools present in all sites and crops were found to be manual, such as machetes (almost 100%) and hoes (50-100%), planting sticks for corn and bean (65%), and post hole diggers for coffee (81.4%). Lowest levels of mechanization occurred in harvesting and post-harvesting, although some machinery for post-harvest coffee processing was present. In western departments, maize shelling and bean threshing are mainly performed manually (up to 90.9%), while in eastern departments a higher usage of mechanical threshers/shellers was observed (up to 85%). The major challenges for production systems reported are the labor shortage, high equipment costs, lack of financing mechanisms, and the need for mechanization solutions adapted to local conditions. The findings suggest that an efficient transformation of production systems in these regions demands scale-appropriate mechanized solutions, paired with strategies that enable a transition from entirely manual tools to small equipment that reduces physical effort of farmers.

title: 43.Simulation of heat-induced spikelet sterility in rice and evaluation of adaptation options under historical and projected meteorological conditions in Japan.
abstract: Context and Objective: Elevated temperatures during the flowering stage can induce spikelet sterility in rice, posing a serious threat to production under climate change. Although several adaptation strategies have been proposed and are under development, their long-term performance under future climatic conditions remains uncertain. This study aimed to estimate heat-induced sterility under historical and projected meteorological conditions in Japan and to evaluate the effectiveness of three adaptation strategies: shifting flowering date, promoting early-morning flowering, and improving heat tolerance. Methods: Historical and future sterility risks were assessed using gridded meteorological datasets. Future projections relied on meteorological data aligned with three greenhouse gas emission scenarios that reflect sustainable growth, middle-of-the-road development, and fossil fuel-dependent trajectories. Sterility rates under historical and projected climates were estimated by computing panicle temperature with a micrometeorological model and applying an established relationship between panicle temperature and sterility. Adaptation effects were quantified by modifying relevant parameters within the simulations. Results and Conclusions: Historical analyses indicated a steady increase in panicle temperature during flowering, with all scenarios showing a similar rise (+0.428°C per decade) until around 2040. A corresponding increase in sterility rate was projected across most regions of Japan, except in the northernmost region (Hokkaido), and was closely associated with the magnitude of warming. Among the adaptation measures, modifying the heading date showed limited benefit, whereas advancing flowering time by 3 h and increasing heat tolerance by 3°C markedly reduced sterility, even under 2050s climate conditions. The combined implementation of early-morning flowering and enhanced heat tolerance exhibited additive effects, with no indication of antagonism. By demonstrating the relative effectiveness of each strategy across future climate scenarios, this study provides important insights into the level of adaptation needed to sustain rice production. Significance: This study offers an early evaluation of heat-induced sterility risks in rice under historical and future climates in Japan, before the issue becomes widespread. By quantifying the effectiveness of major adaptation strategies, the results provide useful guidance for breeding programs seeking to develop heat-tolerant cultivars in anticipation of continued warming.

title: 44.Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence for smart agriculture: a systematic mapping review of sensors, platforms, connectivity, and machine learning applications (2014-2024).
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly integrated to enable datadriven monitoring, prediction, and automation across diverse agricultural systems. This study presents a systematic mapping review of 160 publications published from 2014 onward, identified through a PRISMA-guided process using the Web of Science Core Collection. From 886 retrieved records, deduplication and screening produced a final corpus of 160 eligible studies, which were coded across five system dimensions: (i) sensing targets (the variables measured, e.g., moisture, temperature) and sensor modalities, (ii) embedded hardware and edge platforms, (iii) communication technologies and network protocols, (iv) cloud/data storage and visualization approaches, and (v) AI techniques, models, and application objectives. Results indicate that most implementations adopt a sensor–edge–cloud pipeline, with sensing primarily focused on irrigation and microclimate management. Across reported sensor mentions, soil/substrate moisture (149), air temperature (139), and temperature–humidity sensing (125) are most frequent, followed by air humidity (103) and light intensity (81).At the embedded layer, low-cost prototyping platforms dominate, led by Raspberry Pi (59) and Arduino (55), alongside Wi-Fi enabled microcontrollers such as NodeMCU (32) and ESP8266 (19). Communication choices are strongly concentrated in Wi-Fi (114) and ZigBee (59), with additional recurring use of LoRa, Bluetooth, and MQTT (15 each). Cloud and dashboard solutions are most often implemented using ThingSpeak (26), followed by custom web servers (12) and Blynk (9). AI adoption is primarily machine-learning driven (78.6% of reported AI approaches), with SVM (33) and CNN (23) as the most frequent models. Where stated, AI objectives emphasize prediction (66; 56.4%), followed by classification, detection, and optimization. Among studies reporting deployment context (n = 142), implementations are nearly balanced between open-field (72) and greenhouse/controlled environments (70). Reported crop focus is concentrated in horticulture, particularly tomato (25). Overall, the mapping highlights dominant IoT–AI design patterns while revealing persistent gaps in reporting completeness, interoperability, and coverage of diverse crops and production contexts.

title: 45.Non-persistent virus manipulation increasing host attractiveness is evolutionarily advantageous for transmission by transient and colonising aphids: a mathematical model.
abstract: Non-persistently transmitted (NPT) plant viruses are a major threat to global food security, and are transmitted between plants by aphid vectors, acquired and inoculated through brief epidermal probes. This means they can be vectored by a wide range of aphid species, both those that can feed on and colonise the host ('colonising') and those that cannot ('transient'). Plants infected with NPT viruses often show altered phenotypes which changes the behaviour of the vectors, with two common phenotypes being increased landing attractiveness to infected plants and altered (reduced or increased) plant feeding acceptability. These phenotypes are thought to increase virus transmission through changing aphid vector behaviour, and so have been hypothesised to be deliberate manipulation on the part of the virus. Here, we show that deliberate virus manipulation is plausible by, for the first time, modelling evolution of plant virus manipulation using adaptive dynamics. Through creation of a mathematical model with both a transient and colonising aphid species, we show that increased attraction to infected plants is evolutionarily advantageous for the virus, increasing emigration of infective aphids and increasing virus persistence in the landscape, even when there is a fitness cost to its evolution. We additionally show that virus-induced aphid feeding deterrence or retention can both be advantageous for infective aphid emigration, depending on the carrying capacity of the colonising aphid population. Overall, we provide crucial evidence that these plant host phenotypes could be manipulation on the part of the virus, in order to increase its survival on larger temporal and spatial scales.

title: 46.Earth observations reveal climate-driven expansion of Fusarium wilt risk in cropland.
abstract: Fusarium oxysporumcausesFusariumwilt (FW) in 100+ crops worldwide, yet global risk assessments are limited by sparse surveillance and coarse environmental data. We developed a high-resolution framework integrating 4,524 occurrence records with remotely sensed environmental and host-activity indicators to map present and future FW suitability. An ensemble species distribution model showed that suitability is driven by temperature and soil moisture, and further shaped by cropland extent and host activity inferred from chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). About 20.7% of global land and 70.8% of cropland are currently suitable for FW. CMIP6-based projections indicate net expansion by 2100, driven by warming at mid- to high northern latitudes and by hydrological change and cropland expansion in northern sub-Saharan Africa, while many Southern Hemisphere regions show net losses. By capturing drivers unavailable in conventional datasets, this remote sensing framework represents a step change in global plant disease risk assessment and informs surveillance and management under climate change.

title: 47.When does fungicide use pay off in maize? Evidence from low foliar disease pressure environments in southern Brazil.
abstract: Foliar fungicides are widely used in maize production in southern Brazil, yet their economic justification under low disease pressure remains uncertain. We synthesized yield and economic responses to a fungicide program using a random-effects meta-analytic approach based on 19 multi-environment trials conducted across the first (summer) and second (safrinha) seasons between 2016 and 2020 in Paraná State, Brazil. Trials represented realistic, non-epidemic conditions in which multiple foliar diseases co-occurred at low to moderate intensities. Absolute and relative yield responses were calculated from paired treated and non-treated hybrid plots, and moderator effects of disease pressure and season were evaluated. Fungicide application resulted in a significant yield benefit only when disease was present (>1.6% total severity), with an average difference of 835.5 kg ha-1(95% CI: 484.4-1,186.6). Under disease nearly absent (≤1.6%), the yield response was small and highly uncertain (92.55 kg ha-1; 95% CI: -239.15 to 424.2). Sensitivity analysis based on log response ratios indicated a relative yield difference of 10.1% (95% CI: 3.6-17.0%) when disease was present, while effects across seasons were not statistically significant. Economic simulations showed a 99% probability of positive net return when disease was present compared with only 3% otherwise. Our findings indicate that routine fungicide use in maize is unlikely to be economically justified when disease was nearly absent even when modern premix formulations are applied. These results emphasize the importance of disease-informed decision-making and support targeted, rather than preventive, fungicide applications in maize grown under non-epidemic conditions.

title: 48.Online tool for event and base flow delineation in subsurface drainage - a seasonal threshold approach.
abstract: Accurate separation of Event Flow and Base Flow in subsurface drainage systems is essential for nutrient transport assessment; however, this task remains challenging because both components exist through the same tile network, producing a composite hydrologic signal. This study seeks to establish a standardized, objective, and reproducible method for delineating events and base flows across sites, seasons, and time resolutions. A percentile-based separation framework was developed that applies the 82.5th percentile threshold for wetter seasons, such as winter and spring, and the 95th percentile for drier seasons, such as summer and fall. An event is defined when the flow exceeds the seasonal threshold, increases by at least 20 percent from the previous value, and ends when the flow returns to the threshold for two consecutive time steps. The minimum data requirements of one year for daily datasets and three months for hourly datasets were set to ensure representative flow distributions. A web-based tool was developed to implement the framework, calculate event-scale metrics, and generate reproducible event identifiers. The method produced consistent and repeatable separation of event and base flow and removed the subjective judgments inherent in existing approaches. Overall, this structured and transparent procedure enhances subsurface drainage event-scale hydrologic assessment and supports the improved evaluation of nutrient losses under variable climatic conditions.

title: 49.Genetic structure and spatiotemporal dynamics of Pyricularia oryzae Triticum in Minas Gerais, Brazil.
abstract: Wheat blast is a major threat to wheat production in tropical and subtropical regions of Brazil, yet the influence of epidemiological processes and population genetic structure on epidemic development remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate, across different temporal and spatial scales, the genetic dynamics ofPyricularia oryzaeTriticum lineage populations and their potential role in shaping wheat head blast epidemics. To investigate temporal genetic dynamics, we analyzed 270 isolates collected from wheat and co-occurring grasses at different crop growth stages within a single field. To evaluate potential tissue specialization and regional genetic structuring, an additional 97 isolates from leaves and spikes were sampled in two distinct regions of Minas Gerais. The analyses revealed a predominantly clonal population structure, with identical multilocus genotypes occurring within the same field, across geographic regions, and between plant tissues. The absence of genetic differentiation between leaf- and spike-derived isolates indicates a lack of tissue specialization, suggesting that the same genotypes can infect multiple organs throughout the crop cycle. Moreover, the detection of PoT-positive grasses both before and during wheat development highlights the potential contribution of grass-associated inoculum early in the epidemic. These findings support a scenario of low recombination, strong clonal expansion, and widespread dissemination of a few adapted genotypes, suggesting that early foliar infections and grass-associated inoculum may play a key role in initiating and sustaining wheat blast epidemics.

title: 50.Unpacking the quantitative assessment of bioeconomy system sustainability: gaps, insights, and future pathways.
abstract: Assessing the sustainability of bioeconomy systems is essential to ensure that bioeconomy development is aligned with its strategic goals. Effective assessments must account for the full spectrum of bioeconomy systems considered as a socio-ecological system. Bioeconomy systems are composed of several activities, present specific spatiotemporal dynamics, and are multifunctional by nature. This study presents a systematic literature review of quantitative bioeconomy system sustainability assessments. We selected 93 articles dealing explicitly with bioeconomy systems. Most of the studies concentrated on bioenergy and use life cycle assessment (LCA) methods. However, none evaluated the entire value chain of activities, and downstream processes such as recycling were often overlooked. In addition, few studies considered the detailed practices and processes that critically shape sustainability outcomes. Spatiotemporal dynamics, which are key to understanding system functioning, were rarely addressed. The scope of assessed sustainability criteria was also limited: environmental dimensions were well covered, but economic and social aspects were underexplored. Crucial systemic properties like circularity and resilience were largely absent. These findings reveal significant gaps in current sustainability assessments of bioeconomy systems. Advancing integrated assessment and modelling approaches appears necessary to capture system complexity and support more informed, goal-oriented bioeconomy strategies.

title: 51.Optimization of roasting enhances bioactive profiles, antioxidant activity, and reduces lectin content in bean flours: implications for functional plant-based ingredients.
abstract: BACKGROUND: This study applies Response Surface Methodology (RSM) to optimize roasting temperature (150-220°C) and time (10-20 min) based on the phytochemical, antioxidant, and lectin content of five pulses: cranberry, navy, pinto, yellow beans, and chickpeas, aiming to preserve nutritional quality while reducing antinutrients. RESULTS: Roasting significantly influenced the concentrations of total phenolics, flavonoids, DPPH, FRAP, proanthocyanins, carotenoids, NEPA, and lectins across all cultivars. Optimal roasting was found at 220°C for 20 min, enhancing antioxidant properties, particularly in pigmented beans. Cranberry beans showed the highest total flavonoid (13.1 g kg-1QE DW) and antioxidant activity (DPPH: 50.5%) under optimized conditions. Roasting increased total phenolics in navy (up to 514%) and pinto beans (61.5%), while chickpeas experienced a notable reduction (-66.9%) at 220°C, 20 min. Proanthocyanins and carotenoids were moderately preserved in colored cultivars, while NEPA remained relatively stable. Lectin activity was significantly reduced by more than 85% across all cultivars after soaking and roasting, suggesting improved food safety and digestibility. The RSM models showed good predictive accuracy (R2> 0.80 for most responses), validating the suitability of this approach for optimization. CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the potential of roasting as a minimal, effective processing strategy to enhance the nutritional quality of dry bean flours. The study supports the application of roasted bean flours in health-promoting foods, contributing to the growing demand for functional, plant-based ingredients in food and nutraceutical industries.

title: 52.Application of precision livestock farming: challenges and opportunities.
abstract: Sensor systems have increasingly been explored as tools to support precision livestock farming, particularly in monitoring cow health and improving decision-making. This systematic literature review aims to evaluate advancements in sensor systems for detecting health conditions in dairy cows especially on mastitis, fertility, locomotion, and metabolic disorders. Relevant articles published between 2014 and 2024 were identified from Scopus. Each article was categorized by health condition and assigned to one of four development levels: sensor technique (level I), data interpretation (Level II), integration of information (Level III), and decision making (Level IV). Relevant information from the articles was systematically reviewed and discussed. We identified 132 articles published in the past 10 years, describing a total of 151 sensor systems. Most sensor systems were aimed at mastitis and reproduction, followed by locomotion and metabolic disorders. The far majority of the articles were at level II (data interpretation) presenting research on (novel) algorithms to detect disease. A large number of different statistical or machine-learning or deep-learning models were described and evaluated, amongst others random forests. Level II systems applied statistical analysis or machine-learning/deep-learning models (e.g., random forests, You Only Look Once (YOLO), Support Vector Machine (SVM), or Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)). These algorithms did use a wide range of sensor data. Only few articles aimed at level III research, integration of information and decision support. The Level III sensor systems integrated information from the sensor with economic information and other information i.e., medication dosage, cost per disease, supplier selection, and simulates various treatment scenarios. This review highlights the need for sensor systems research to be driven by real-world requirements for on-farm decision making. To move from proof-of-concept toward practical, future research must integrate sensor outputs with herd records and financial models, validate systems across multiple farms and at higher data frequencies, and embed economic evaluation alongside sensitivity and specificity metrics. Addressing these technical, integration, and economic challenges is essential before sensor systems can fully support automated, value-driven health management on commercial dairy farms.

title: 53.Limits to growth in global crop yield? Insights from data mining of the FAOSTAT database from 1961 to 2023.
abstract: We conducted a comprehensive data mining analysis of the FAOSTAT database to assess historical trends and current limits in global crop yield development. The study included 157 major crops across 202 countries from 1961 to 2023, focusing on time series of yield (t/ha) and area harvested (ha). Weighted global average yields and annual maximum yields were calculated for each crop and classified into four categories of temporal evolution: never improved, still increasing, stagnating, and decreasing. Over the study period, total crop production rose by a factor of 3.9, primarily driven by a 2.54-fold increase in average yield, with harvested area contributing a smaller share. Analysis revealed that approximately 77% of global production volume remains in the "still increasing" category for average yield, although this share has declined from previous decades. In contrast, only about a quarter of production volume continues to experience increases in maximum yield, suggesting a growing number of crops nearing biophysical yield limits. Yield-area diagrams, categorized by a semi-quantitative "L-chart" approach, indicate that high yields are predominantly restricted to relatively small harvested areas, with over 90% of crops showing strong spatial limitations to yield scalability. These findings imply that opportunities for further global crop production expansion via yield improvement are increasingly constrained, and that recent output gains have largely depended on continued expansion of harvested area.

title: 54.Genetic diversity of South American oil-palm Acrocomia totai Mart. (Arecaceae) across the total area of occurrence reveals the true distribution of existing populations.
abstract: Acrocomiapalms are neotropical species endemic to the Americas that are of significant interest as a source of oil.Acrocomia totaiis among the most common palm species in the central region of South America and is well adapted to subtropical conditions, but has never been investigated across the whole area of its natural distribution. The objective of the present work was to assess the genomic diversity ofA. totaiin the total area of distribution, for which we sequenced genomic DNA from dried-leaf material by genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) and subsequently analyzed SNP variants to make geographic inferences. We identified four distinct genomic populations: west (west Bolivia and northwest Argentina), northeast (parts of west Brazil), central (north Paraguay, east Bolivia and parts of west Brazil) and south (northeast Argentina and south Paraguay) populations. The genomic populations did not overlap with each other to a large extent, showing a parapatric distribution, and there was a good correspondence between geographic distribution and genomic structure. The populations were clearly structured, with the most divergent population in the west largely geographically separated from the other populations by the Boreal dry Chaco semi-arid region. Genomic diversity between populations was higher than within populations. The individuals that form the northeast population are suspected to be natural hybrids withA. aculeata. The central population was the most diverse and may possibly represent the origin for the species. Our biodiversity study provides useful information for further phylogenetic, ecological, taxonomic and agronomic studies, and supports local strategies for management and conservation.

title: 55.Foliar delivery in privet (Ligustrum spp.) via selective laser cuticle ablation coupled with a reservoir patch.
abstract: Foliar application offers a direct pathway for delivering active compounds to plants, yet the waxy leaf cuticle forms a strong diffusion barrier that limits uptake. The Foliar Laser Boost (FLB) + Patch method provides a controlled approach for low-residue foliar delivery: a low-power diode laser creates microscale permeability windows in the cuticle without injuring underlying tissues, and a biodegradable hydrogel patch maintains localized contact and confinement of the applied solution to sustain uptake. To demonstrate feasibility in privet (Ligustrumspp.) (Ligustrumspp.), we used Opulent Zn as a model fertilizer under a single optical recipe (450 nm, 4.5 W, ~1.06 m s-1, +7 mm defocus). The Laser + Patch treatment increased leaf Zn relative to control and laser-only under identical dosing (ICP-OES on pooled leaves; n=1 composite per treatment). These results support a dose-governed, minimally invasive delivery mechanism in privet (Ligustrumspp.). FLB + Patch may be extendable to nutrients, hormones, biostimulants, and other foliar agents, offering a practical and potentially scalable pathway to improve dose efficiency while limiting off-target residues.

title: 56.Evaluation of paddy-pisciculture hybrid farming (PPHF) in the Yamuna plains of India.
abstract: This study proposes a novel approach, Paddy Pisciculture Hybrid Farming (PPHF), to address the challenge of elevated basicity levels in conventional paddy-pisciculture fields. PPHF integrates fish breeding into paddy cultivation in a hybrid setup, increasing productivity and efficiency in agroecosystems. Our proposed model involves a trench system, pH detectors, and water valves mapped to an alert system. After implementing and analyzing the PPHF system in the Yamuna plains of India, it could be concluded that it is a one-stop-shop solution for combating farmer poverty since it produces four times the conventional fish yield and healthier paddy crops along with urea-rich water which can either find its way onto the river streams promoting sustainability or it can be further utilized to produce nitrogen fertilizers.

title: 57.Global climate and biodiversity targets on a limited and used planet.
abstract: To mitigate the ongoing ecological and climate crisis, governments and private actors are developing multiple interventions, among which three have large implications on land: (i) conservation of natural ecosystems, (ii) forest and landscapes restoration and afforestation and (iii) non-fossil energy production, through renewable energy infrastructures and the associated minerals mining, and land-based bioenergy. Expanding the area devoted to these sustainability interventions can lead to conflicts between these and with other land uses. We compiled quantitative targets from multilateral agreements or public commitments, and, using global suitability and priority maps, provide a spatial assessment of their distribution and overlap at the global level. We found that meeting global sustainability targets would require more than doubling the area already occupied by the considered interventions, to reach a total of ~5350 Mha in 2050, or ~40% of the ice-free land surface (of which 30% for conservation). A third of current agricultural land, and over half of the forestry land would be targeted in 2050 if the interventions were spatialized following a top-down and siloed approach, with large country and regional disparities. Over a third of energy-related best-locations are also targeted by other interventions. When also considering other business-as-usual land demands for food, fiber and timber, taken together with sustainability interventions, the area needed is larger than the earth's ice-free land surface. Our findings provide additional insight into the mounting land squeeze, and stress the need to break silos, and focus on organising sobriety to reduce production and overconsumption.
authors: Erasmus K. H. J. zu Ermgassen

title: 58.Micropropagación in vitro de Lavandula angustifolia con 6-bencilaminopurina y Kinetina.
59.Climate-smart aquaculture and fisheries practices and technologies in West and Central Africa: a systematic review.
abstract: Climate change poses significant challenges to the sustainability of aquaculture and fisheries production in West and Central Africa, sectors that are critical for food security, nutrition, and livelihoods. Despite the region's rapid aquatic food production growth, overall production remains low compared to global levels, while capture fisheries remain dominant but highly vulnerable to climate variability. In this study, we conducted a systematic review of climate-smart aquaculture and fisheries (CSAF) technologies and practices in West and Central Africa, following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. From 359 publications retrieved, 90 studies, covering the period 2008-2023 met our inclusion criteria. Using a multi-criteria framework, aquaculture and fisheries technologies and practices identified were assessed for their contribution to the three pillars of climate-smart agriculture (CSA): productivity, adaptation, and mitigation. Results highlight recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), Biofloc technology, water reuse and treatment systems, and integrated models such as aquaponics and integrated aquaculture-agriculture as the most promising climate-smart aquaculture practices. In fisheries, ecosystem-based fisheries management (EBFM) and protected areas management (PAMs) emerged as the climate-smart approaches. However, adoption remains uneven across countries, constrained by limited finance, weak institutional capacity, fragmented policies, and low access to extension services. This suggests that while technological solutions are essential, building resilient aquatic food systems in the region hinges on strategic public investments, effective risk reduction, and strengthened intergovernmental governance.

title: 60.Foliar delivery via selective laser ablation of the leaf cuticle coupled with a reservoir patch.
abstract: Foliar application offers a direct and efficient pathway for delivering active compounds to plants. However, the waxy cuticle that protects leaves also acts as a strong diffusion barrier, drastically limiting the uptake of most substances. The Foliar Laser Boost (FLB) + Patch method introduces a novel, potentially generalizable approach for controlled, minimal-residue foliar delivery. A low-power diode laser locally ablates micro-windows in the cuticle without damaging underlying tissues, while a biodegradable hydrogel patch maintains prolonged contact and confinement of the applied compound, supporting high uptake under the tested conditions. To demonstrate the concept, Opulent Zn fertilizer was used as a model fertilizer and tested on morphologically distinct crops-grapevine (Vitis vinifera) and blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum). In both cases, the laser + patch combination produced a several-fold increase in uptake relative to conventional spray application, confirming the method's reproducibility and adaptability. The FLB + Patch system thus represents a universal, sustainable platform for delivering nutrients, hormones, biostimulants, or other foliar-applied agents with unprecedented efficiency and precision.

title: 61.Buckwheat does not make honey bees more defensive.
abstract: Beekeepers in eastern North America commonly report that honey bees foraging on buckwheat are more defensive in the afternoon than when foraging on other pollen and nectar sources. We sought to document this phenomenon quantitatively and identify the causes of this observation. The trial during the typical buckwheat-crop season in New York had three hives adjacent to a field of buckwheat large enough to satisfy all their resource demands. The measurements included honey bee foraging activity on buckwheat throughout the day, the coincident return of resources to the hive and defensiveness. Honey bees foraged actively on the buckwheat throughout the day, collecting both nectar and pollen. Buckwheat pollen was only available in the morning, but nectar was available all day. Each colony also foraged on other species even when buckwheat was more easily available. Colonies were not more defensive in the afternoon. However, when the buckwheat resource was removed, they became more defensive than they were when foraging on buckwheat. These results show that honey bees do not show high fidelity to buckwheat, but that they use a wide variety of resources. We did not find that they were more defensive in the afternoon when foraging on buckwheat. Buckwheat flowers at the time of year when there is commonly a resource dearth in the region and we suggest that the increased defensiveness observed by beekeepers is more likely due to the resource dearth and increased risk of robbing, than to buckwheat foraging.

title: 62.Redesigning photosynthesis: a machine learning simulation and synthetic strategies to enhance carbon, water, and nitrogen efficiency in crops.
abstract: Improving photosynthetic efficiency in C3crops such as rice, wheat, and soybean remains a global priority for enhancing yield and resource use under climate stress. The major biochemical and physiological bottlenecks limiting photosynthesis include energy loss through photorespiration, the slow catalytic rate and thermal instability of Rubisco, and suboptimal stomatal regulation that drives excessive water loss. Here, we present a computational simulation integrating photorespiration bypass (PB), Rubisco optimisation (RO), and stomatal tuning (ST) to evaluate their combined impacts on photosynthetic performance under 10,000 realistic environmental scenarios. Each intervention was parameterized using literature-derived benchmarks and analyzed using a Random Forest regression framework. Our results predict average increases of 14.6% in net CO2assimilation (ΔAnet), 9.3% in water-use efficiency (ΔWUE), and 10.8% in nitrogen-use efficiency (ΔNUE) relative to baseline wild-type performance. Rubisco optimisation emerged as the dominant driver of carbon assimilation, while photorespiration bypass provided the largest biomass gains under high temperature and light. Stomatal tuning amplified overall performance by improving WUE under high vapor pressure deficit. These findings highlight the importance of integrating biochemical, enzymatic, and physiological engineering to overcome the inherent inefficiencies of C3photosynthesis. The framework offers a quantitative roadmap for predictive crop design and systems-level photosynthetic improvement, supporting the development of climate-resilient food crops for sustainable agriculture.

title: 63.Agrivoltaics as a systems innovation: multi-dimensional benefits from global studies across climate, agriculture, energy, and ecosystems.
abstract: Agrivoltaics offers a promising alternative to land competition between crops and solar farms. Most agrivoltaic research and policy discourse, however, has focused on energy yield and food output, overlooking the broader spectrum of ecological, economic, and social that has made it challenging to fully assess agrivoltaics' potential as a comprehensive systems-level solution. This study addresses this gap by synthesizing findings from prior studies and categorizing their insights into six distinct but interconnected spheres of agrivoltaic impact: Sustainability Sphere (Water-Climate-Ecosystem), Soil Crop Sphere (Agricultural Yield and Food Security), Socioeconomic Sphere (Economic and Financial Resilience), Solar Power Sphere (Energy and Power Generation), Spatial Efficiency Sphere (Land Productivity & Land Use Synergies), and Species Sphere (Human and Animal Welfare). The evidence demonstrates that implementing agrivoltaics across crops that demonstrated yield increases could generate an additional 1,800 million tonnes of food globally, which could feed more than 2.1 billion people annually. Such a scale of impact suggests that agrivoltaics could be instrumental in reducing global hunger and mitigating starvation-related deaths, especially in regions most vulnerable to food insecurity. Economically, the increased agricultural output could generate over $1 trillion USD in additional agriculture income, bolstering rural livelihoods, national economies, and global trade. Agrivoltaics not only promotes more efficient land use but also reduces water demand and carbon emissions by partially shading crops, thereby mitigating the negative effects of climate change on yield and irrigation needs. It is clear that agrivoltaics is a multidimensional solution with far-reaching global implications.

title: 64.Review of multitrophic interactions mediated by volatile compounds in rice inoculated with Beauveria bassiana: effects on Spodoptera spp. and Trichogramma parasitoids.
abstract: Rice production faces significant losses fromSpodoptera frugiperda, with current control strategies relying heavily on chemical insecticides and Bt cultivars, leading to resistance development and environmental concerns. This systematic review examined multitrophic interactions mediated by volatile organic compounds (VOCs) inOryza sativainoculated with the entomopathogenic fungusBeauveria bassiana, evaluating impacts on army wormsSpodopteraspp. and parasitoids of the genus Trichogramma parasitoids. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, 20 studies from 2000-2025 were analyzed. The results indicated thatB. bassianaendophytic colonization modulates VOC profiles, including emission of green leaf volatiles, monoterpenes (e.g., α-pinene), and sesquiterpenes (e.g., β-caryophyllene), enhancing parasitoid attraction and reducing pest oviposition and larval survival. The review also identified fungal VOCs, such as 3-methylbutanol, with direct behavioral effects on pests. Bibliometric analysis revealed increasing research interest but thematic fragmentation between applied entomopathogen studies and chemical ecology. Despite evidence supporting VOC-mediated indirect plant defenses, methodological limitations persist, including insufficient compound characterization and limited field validation. This synthesis underscored the potential of integrating endophytic entomopathogenic fungi to manipulate plant chemical signaling, offering a promising strategy for sustainable and ecologically based pest management in rice cultivation, particularly in tropical agroecosystems.

title: 65.Consistent high body condition in meat ewes is associated with long survival rates and high lifetime productivity: a seven-year prospective longitudinal study of 6000 ewes from eleven flocks in England.
abstract: Improving the lifetime productivity of ewes is important to improve efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from sheep farming. In 2017, eleven English sheep flocks with 6000 nulliparous ewes were enrolled into a seven-year prospective longitudinal study to investigate lifetime performance of ewes joining the flock as ewe lambs or shearlings over six parities. Multivariable statistical models were used to investigate productivity and survival of ewes per year and over 6-years of production, adjusting for confounding variables. The key results were: lifetime performance of ewes was dependent on their survival for all six parities; ewes mated as ewe lambs (6-7 months old) produced approximately one lamb more over their lifetime than ewes mated as shearlings (18-20 months old); and ewe survival, litter size, lamb weight gain to eight-weeks and to weaning, increased, as ewe body condition at mating that season increased. Productivity plateaued in ewes with body condition score 4.0 on a 1-5 point scale, higher than reported previously. Weight gain from mating to mid-pregnancy also increased productivity, especially in ewe lambs. This is the longest prospective study of ewe performance in England, and it highlights that maximum productivity occurs in sheep with a consistent body condition score of 4.0. The results can be used by the sheep industry together with input factors, such as farm location, sheep breed, feeding and other costs, to optimise lifetime performance of ewes in different systems.

title: 66.Cowpea postharvest losses under smallholder farmer management in Benin: extent, causes and opportunities.
abstract: Cowpea is a vital source of dietary protein for millions of people across sub-Saharan Africa. The crop is typically grown by smallholder farmers for household consumption and to generate income through sales. However, postharvest losses are perceived to be high affecting both the quantity and quality of cowpea available. To design targeted loss reduction activities, understanding is needed of the extent, causes and activity stages during which losses occur. The cowpea postharvest systems of 120 farming households across four agro-ecological zones of Benin were explored across two years through interviews. Additionally, directly measured loss assessments at each activity stage from harvest to store loading and during a 6-month storage period were done with a subset of these households. Postharvest activities were mainly done manually. Storage practices included storing untreated grains in woven polypropylene (PP) bags or plastic or metal drums, or treatment of cowpea grains with synthetic chemical pesticide dust, a fumigant or dried chilli and storage in PP bags. Measurement found the cumulative mean quantity losses from harvesting through six months of storage were 19.03-21.96% with the highest proportion of these losses occurring during harvesting (3.34-3.89%), drying of pods (1.96-2.05%), threshing (3.22-3.71%), and storage (10.14-12.01%). Loss levels were similar between years. Loss causes included rainfall during harvesting and/or drying, poor threshing methods, labour shortages, storage insect pest attack and rotting. An opportunity clearly exists for targeted multi-stakeholder participatory action research to co-develop affordable and acceptable ways of reducing these significant losses of such nutritionally and economically important grain legumes.

title: 67.Urban farms represent highly heterogenous management environments, complicating on-farm food safety efforts.
abstract: Urban agriculture is increasingly promoted for its contributions to food access, equity, and sustainability, yet food safety risks in these systems remain underexplored in the United States. To address this gap, we surveyed 43 urban growers across 12 cities in the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Southeast U.S. Semi-structured interviews, field walk-throughs, and follow-up reviews were used to characterize farm practices, land use histories, infrastructure, and grower perspectives on microbial and chemical hazards. Findings revealed heterogeneity in practices and farm histories between and within farms. Many farms prioritized community empowerment, education, and food access. Growers frequently expressed concern about legacy chemical contamination but reported limited training or awareness of microbial hazards. Structural constraints such as insecure land tenure, limited resources, reliance on volunteers and donated materials, and staff turnover further complicated consistent implementation of food safety measures. These results highlight the limits of applying rural, commercial farm-oriented food safety frameworks to urban farm contexts. Improving food safety outcomes in urban agriculture will require flexible, field-specific risk assessments, alongside policies and technical assistance that address both knowledge gaps and structural barriers facing urban growers.

title: 68.Laser-induced cuticle removal improves foliar zinc uptake in row crops.
abstract: We evaluate a handheld 450 nm continuous-wave laser (FLB-02, Onteko Inc., Olive Branch, MS, USA) to selectively remove epicuticular wax on leaves of zucchini, cowpea, okra, and cotton, and quantify 24-h zinc (Zn) uptake by ICP-OES. Screening identified a forgiving working window at 1.33 m/s (~3-4 W) delivering uniform, non-destructive ablation. Laser-assisted foliar application increased Zn in contralateral leaves across species, consistent with facilitated entry followed by species-dependent redistribution. The results suggest a practical, field-ready approach to enhance foliar nutrient use efficiency.

title: 69.Weather-driven ensemble logistic models for predicting Fusarium head blight of wheat in Brazil.
abstract: Fusariumhead blight (FHB), caused by members of theFusarium graminearumspecies complex, is a major constraint to wheat production in southern Brazil. In this study, we used a functional data analysis (FDA) framework to identify critical weather variables around the flowering period, and guide the development of risk models predicting an epidemic (FHB > 10% severity; n = 125 cases) evaluated in terms of predictive performance and economic benefit. FDA revealed that daily records of mean relative humidity, mean minimum temperature, precipitation, and mean dew point temperature, summarized as average or totals, particularly within 2 to 10 days after the beginning of flowering, were strongly associated with epidemic risk. These insights informed logistic regression models, either assuming linear effects or incorporating restricted cubic splines to account for potential non-linearities. All individual models showed good predictive performance (ROC-AUC 0.79-0.81). Ensemble approaches further improved discrimination (ROC-AUC up to 0.84), with the stacked ensemble providing the best balance between sensitivity, specificity, and probability calibration, thus representing the most reliable option for forecasting. When economic implications on the use of the stacked ensemble were assessed using a Net Monetary Benefit (NMB) framework, the probability of achieving a positive NMB surpassed 80% at risk probability thresholds ≥0.45, indicating that fungicide applications are economically justified at moderate to high epidemic risk levels. The simplified models developed here, based on summaries of daily weather during peak flowering, may serve as practical tools to support FHB management decisions under southern Brazilian conditions.

title: 70.Wheat diseases and pests in Pakistan: a nationwide assessment.
abstract: Wheat production in Pakistan faces persistent threats from diseases and pests. However, limited geographic information exists on local risks, economic impacts, and management practices. We used expert knowledge elicitation to provide the first integrated assessment of wheat health in Pakistan. Experts mapped yield losses for major diseases and pests at the district level. We analyzed networks of seed and grain exchange and stakeholder interactions. Analysis of wheat cropland connectivity identified locations that are likely to play important epidemiological roles. Cumulative yield losses estimated by experts ranged from 4% to 16%, with hotspots in central Punjab and northern Sindh. Stripe rust, leaf rust, and aphids remained top threats, with climate change and pathogen population structure identified as likely major determinants of yield losses. Experts indicated that there were national networks of informal wheat seed and grain exchange, highlighting key pathways for potential spread of seedborne pathogens. In stakeholder networks characterized by experts, farmer associations and seed dealers were strategic points for information sharing and seed health monitoring. Cropland connectivity analysis identified highly connected wheat areas along the Indus River, overlapping with national disease hotspots and facilitating pathogen proliferation. Pakistan has a moderate vulnerability to wheat blast introduction, yet climate change and informal seed movement could increase this potential. These findings provide farmer associations, researchers, and policymakers with actionable control points to enhance wheat health systems in Pakistan. This study establishes a rapid information baseline to support geographically targeted surveillance, spatial disease-resistance deployment, coordinated seed system interventions, and epidemic preparedness planning.

title: 71.Is field size an indicator of farm size in smallholder-dominated croplands?
abstract: Farm size is a key characteristic of agricultural systems, closely linked to farming and land management practices. However, data on farm size are often difficult to obtain, especially in smallholder-dominated regions, and where available, they are rarely spatially explicit. This study examines the use of field size as a proxy for farm size, aiming to identify field size thresholds that can distinguish farms of different sizes. Using household-level data from Zambia’s Crop Forecast Survey (CFS), we applied both continuous and categorical methods to quantify the field-to-farm size relationship (FFR). Non-parametric Theil–Sen regression revealed a generally linear relationship between log-transformed field and farm sizes, particularly at the survey enumeration area (SEA) scale, where farm size is proportional to field size (slope ≈ 1) and field size alone predicts farm size with a median bias of 0.017 ha. A Gaussian Naive Bayes classifier was also developed to assign fields to three categories: very small (A: < 2 ha), small (B: 2–5 ha), and medium (C: 5–20 ha), and a coarser two-class scheme (S: < 5 ha; M: 5–20 ha) that has been applied in previous studies. The Gaussian model identified field size thresholds at 0.58–0.6 ha (A–B) and 1.18–1.69 ha (B–C), depending on the prior farm size distribution. For the S–M scheme, thresholds ranged from 0.96–1.4 ha. Using these thresholds, national classification achieved F1 scores of 0.78, 0.59, and 0.77 for A, B, and C, respectively, with B more prone to misclassification. The two-class model achieved 0.87 and 0.88 for S and M, indicating more robust classification performance under a coarser scheme. Kernel density analysis shows that field-size distributions within farm categories and the separability of these distributions, vary across regions, with the underlying factors responsible for these differences remaining an open question for future research. These results demonstrate the potential of field size as a spatial proxy for farm size to support remote sensing based farming system classification in data-scarce regions.

title: 72.Optical screening technique for detecting Tospovirus infection in capsicum seeds.
abstract: Tospovirus infections in capsicum crops pose a serious threat to agricultural productivity, as infected seeds often appear visually indistinguishable from healthy ones. While conventional detection techniques such as DAS-ELISA offer high accuracy, they are time-consuming, labour-intensive, and require skilled personnel. This study proposes a non-invasive, non-destructive optical screening method for the rapid detection of Tospovirus-infected capsicum seeds. Optical sensor system integrates a custom-designed hardware setup comprising photodiodes and colour sensors illuminated by white and infrared light emitting diodes to capture reflectance data across red, green, blue, and infrared spectral bands. These reflectance signatures were processed using a Random Forest classification algorithm to distinguish infected seeds from healthy ones. Experimental results showed that the green spectral band delivered the highest classification performance, with an accuracy of 0.95, precision of 0.9667, recall of 0.9355, and F1 score of 0.9508. Red band also performed well, achieving 0.9 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.9062. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed optical screening approach as a rapid, accurate, and scalable method for early-stage detection of Tospovirus in seeds, offering a viable alternative to traditional diagnostics.

title: 73.Peace lily-mediated biofiltration of indoor ammonia and VOCs at elevated concentrations.
abstract: This study explores the phytoremediation potential of indoor plants under extreme air pollution conditions, employing a custom-built wireless sensor system based on the ESP32 microcontroller and integrated with the Blynk mobile platform for real-time monitoring. A sealed glass chamber was used to simulate a confined indoor environment with high concentrations (2500 ppm and 3500 ppm) of airborne pollutants - namely ammonia, formaldehyde, benzene, and toluene - far exceeding typical exposure levels in existing phytoremediation studies. The peace lily, selected for its established air-purifying properties, demonstrated the highest remediation efficacy against ammonia, with reductions of 51.3% and 64% at 2500 ppm and 3500 ppm, respectively. These reductions were accompanied by increased transpiration rates of 48% and 38%, indicating active physiological responses. Experimental results suggest pollutant-specific detoxification pathways, with ammonia predominantly processed via the glutamine synthetase pathway and other volatile organic compounds through oxidative and conjugative mechanisms. This study highlights the potential of peace lily as a resilient botanical candidate for improving air quality in highly polluted indoor environments and underscores the value of integrating smart monitoring technologies with plant-based air purification strategies.

title: 74.WeedFormer: context-enhanced semantic segmentation for precise weed detection in RGB agricultural imagery.
abstract: With the rapid development of precision agriculture, field weed recognition technology has become a key component for improving crop yields and reducing herbicide usage. This paper focuses on high-precision weed detection in agricultural scenarios and proposes a semantic segmentation model named WeedFormer. By introducing a cross-scale contextual attention mechanism and a dual-scale consistency supervision strategy, WeedFormer significantly enhances the modeling capability of complex field semantic structures. On three representative farmland image datasets - BoniRob, CWFID, and Rice - WeedFormer improves the IoU metric to 88.76%, 86.38%, and 88.11%, respectively, achieving gains of more than 2.3 percentage points over mainstream models such as SegFormer and SegMAN. Meanwhile, the F1-score reaches 91.59%, 88.65%, and 90.77%, demonstrating outstanding structural preservation and boundary recognition capabilities. This research provides a strong algorithmic foundation for the visual perception modules in agricultural robots and intelligent farming machinery, showing great potential for practical applications.

title: 75.Self-cover cropping systems and the plusquam-annual: new paradigms for sustainable food production.
abstract: Annual grain production is vital for food security, but fallow periods punctuating annual crop cultivation are environmentally problematic. While cover cropping offers a solution, implementation carries significant practical hurdles. Here we introduce self-cover cropping systems - achieved through post-harvest crop regrowth - to deliver cover crop-like ecosystem services with fewer challenges. As a corollary, we defineplusquam-annuals (meaning "more than annuals") as a distinct, novel crop growth habit characterized by a single grain harvest followed by regrowth. We suggest viable self-cover cropping cereals may already exist and offer a conceptual framework that invites empirical exploration with both applied and theoretical significance.

title: 76.Modeling yield loss associated with the corn stunt disease complex using an ordinal severity scale
abstract: Historically considered of secondary importance, the corn stunt disease complex, caused by mollicutes and viruses, has recently become an increasing concern in Brazil. In this study, we quantified the relationship between disease severity, measured using a 1–6 quantitative ordinal scale, and corn yield (kg/ha) using data from 22 independent field trials (72 different hybrids) conducted by IDR-Paraná across 10 municipalities in Paraná State over two growing seasons. These trials were analyzed jointly using a random-coefficients mixed-effects model fitted to yield as a function of disease severity, allowing for both random intercepts and slopes across studies. The model explained 80.4% of the total variance in yield (conditional R² = 0.80), of which 18.9% was attributable to the fixed effect of severity (marginal R² = 0.19). The adjusted intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC = 0.76) indicated that most of the variability occurred among studies rather than within studies. The estimated attainable yield was 8,227 kg/ha, and yield declined by 1,043 kg/ha for each unit increase in severity, equivalent to an average 12.7% yield reduction per severity score unit. At the highest severity level, yield losses reached approximately 63% relative to symptom-free plots. The two-level categorical covariates hybrid tolerance and hybrid susceptibility did not significantly affect the slope of the relationship, indicating a consistent yield response to increasing disease severity across hybrids. These findings highlight the substantial and predictable impact of the corn stunt disease complex on corn yield under field conditions in southern Brazil.

title: 77.The epidemiology of wild-crop interfaces: integrating ecology, evolution, and management through modeling.
abstract: Plant diseases occurring across wild and crop plants present modeling and management challenges. Wild plant and crop pathosystems differ in ecological structure, evolutionary dynamics and responsiveness to human intervention. At the interface, pathogens may spill over, spill back, persist, or evolve, shaped by host diversity, dispersal processes, and landscape connectivity. The potential importance of factors including pathogen dispersal, host life history, and spatial configuration are examined through a qualitative comparison of case studies:Puccinia graminis,Phakopsora pachyrhizi,Xylella fastidiosa,Pyricularia oryzaeTriticum lineage, andAustropuccinia psidii. These examples illustrate how wild hosts may function as reservoirs, recombination partners or spillover targets, and how their role influences management efficacy and evolutionary risk. We explore the consequences of this wild–crop interface through two central questions: (1) how should plant diseases involving wild and cultivated pathosystems be managed, and (2) what proportion of management effort should be allocated to each system? We show the principles underpinning answers to these questions via a conceptual framework based on a generic compartmental model incorporating asymmetric transmission and system-specific interventions, thereby accounting for key aspects of pathogen spread within and between wild host and crop populations. Finally, we identify critical data needs and modeling directions to better inform disease management on the wild plant-crop interface and argue for a more integrative approach bridging ecological and anthropogenic drivers of epidemics.

title: 78.Six-year field evaluation of the defense inducing biofungicide Bacillus mycoides isolate J for grapevine downy and powdery mildew control.
abstract: Biofungicides have emerged as a low-resistance risk alternative to conventional fungicides for managing grapevine (Vitisspp.) diseases due to their diverse and novel modes of action. Microbial biofungicides that control disease by up regulating plant defenses have garnered particular interest. Longitudinal product performance assessment is key to understanding how defense upregulating biofungicides can successfully integrate into traditional vineyard disease management programs. From 2017 through 2022, we evaluated the defense inducing, microbial biofungicideBacillus mycoidesisolate J (BmJ, trade name LifeGard® WG, FRAC group P06) in programs alongside conventional fungicides for grapevine downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola) and powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator) control inV. viniferacv. Chardonnay andV.interspecific hybrid cv. Chancellor research vineyards in Geneva, NY. Disease incidence and severity were evaluated on leaves and clusters at harvest using a modified Horsfall-Barratt rating scale. Results showed that treatments incorporating BmJ significantly reduced disease incidence and severity compared to the untreated control, however the degree of control depended upon overall disease pressure. Generally, conventional materials provided more effective control than BmJ-only treatments. However, programs that used BmJ in rotation with conventional fungicides provided end-of-season disease control equivalent to programs containing only conventional fungicides, for both diseases. These findings suggest that integrating the microbial biofungicide BmJ into traditional vineyard disease management programs can reduce overall conventional chemistry usage while maintaining effective disease control. Ultimately, integrating efficacious biofungicides into traditional vineyard disease management programs may help slow the rate of fungicide resistance development with no loss of disease control.

title: 79.Enhancing plant pathology discovery and application development through automated, high-throughput hyperspectral imaging.
abstract: Hyperspectral sensing has emerged in recent years as a powerful tool for discovery in plant pathology. However, bottlenecks in reflectance data collection, including throughput and data handling, hinder the speed at which this technology can transition from niche to widespread use, and its downstream applications from proof-of-concept to proof-of-practice. We developed an automated high-throughput hyperspectral imaging (AHHI) platform to address this challenge. Our system includes a push broom hyperspectral camera (MSV500, Middleton Spectral Vision; 400-1000 nm, 8 nm spatial and 0.65 nm spectral resolution) and a sample positioning automatic system inherited from "Blackbird," a microscopic imaging robotic platform. The system acquires line images at 100 frames per sec, equivalent to about 40 sec per 10-mm leaf disc sample (4 hours per 351 samples). The output of the system is 2.5 GB *.raw and *.hdr files, which are processed by an in-house Python script. Our system can collect 9 TB of high-quality hyperspectral images in a single day without external variation in imagery. We demonstrate three use cases for scaling established hyperspectral reflectance applications to the imaging scale via the AHHI: pre-symptomatic disease detection, fungicide detection, and grapevine breeding family lineage discrimination. PERMANOVA and Random Forest analysis all yielded significant p-values and AUC ranging from 77.8 to 99.9%, mirroring prior accuracies from handheld spectrometers. Access to large amounts of high-resolution hyperspectral data with systems such as AHHI can ease and accelerate translation of plant pathology discoveries from niche to mainstream use.

title: 80.Reinventing artisanal curry leaf paste: biochemical and sensory analysis of five distinct Sri Lankan cultivars.
abstract: Spices and condiments bring unique flavors to food, with curry leaves being prominent condiment in Asian cuisines. In Sri Lanka, several Rutaceae family plants are referred to as "curry plants." This study examined the chemical, proximate, phytochemical, and sensory properties of selected curry plant cultivars. Buffalo curry plant (Clausena indicaOliv.) and Purple curry plant (putative variant ofMurraya koenigii), demonstrated superior nutritional qualities, exhibiting significantly higher levels of polyphenol and antioxidant than Common curry plant [Murraya koenigii(L.) Spreng.]. Leaf oil analysis identified shared compounds, including α-humulene, α-pinene, α-selinene, β-elemene, β-caryophyllene, β-pinene, caryophyllene oxide, and 2, 3, 4, 6-tetramethoxy-styrene. Exclusive sensory evaluation ofC. indicaand Purple curry leaves uncovered a preference forC. indica, likely due to its higher eucalyptol content (29.6%) contributing to a more appealing aroma compared to Purple curry leaves' predominant β-caryophyllene content (32.4%). These findings guide future food product development and potential nutraceutical applications.
authors: S. M. C. U. P. Subasinghe

title: 81.A randomized controlled field trial of an adhesive gel bandage in addition to topical antibiotic treatment of digital dermatitis in dairy cows.
abstract: Background: Digital dermatitis (DD) is a painful disease causing lameness in dairy cows worldwide, accounting for 32% of all lesions identified at foot trimming in the UK (1). Enhanced control measures would improve welfare and reduce economic impact. Treatment with bandages as an adjunct to topical antimicrobials appears effective (2) but requires additional labour to change dressings, and may pose problems in wet environments. A novel waterproof adhesive gel bandage removes the need for dressing change and protects from external moisture. This study investigated the efficacy of this adhesive gel bandage in combination with topical antibiotics in the treatment of digital dermatitis. Methods: This randomised, controlled field trial compared an adhesive gel bandage over topical chlortetracycline spray (CTC) versus CTC alone in DD cases on three dairy farms. Treatment was applied at 0 and 7 days with DD Mortellaro score (M-score) and locomotion score evaluated at 0,7 and 28 days. Results: Lesions treated with a combination of the CTC and the adhesive gel bandage showed a significantly higher probability of lesion improvement at day 7 (OR 2.45 (95%CI:1.74-5.12), p=0.017) and 28 (OR 3.37 (95%CI 1.12-10.13), p=0.03,) and of cure at day 28 (OR 3.38 (95%CI 1.12-10.13), p=0.03,), compared with the control. Although most lesions in the treatment group improved in lesion score (84.3%), only 30.4% (range 24.5-37.8% by farm) achieved complete cure. Limitations: The study was carried out on three commercial dairy units which may not be replicable in all systems. The M-score cure rates at 28 days suggest a need for further revision of protocols to improve cure rates. Conclusion: The addition of an adhesive gel bandage in the topical treatment of DD on commercial dairy farms significantly improved healing and probability of cure.

title: 82.Within- and cross-regional crop classification for cool climate upland agriculture using AlphaEarth.
abstract: Accurate crop classification is essential for precision agriculture, policy making, and environmental monitoring. While Google AlphaEarth provides powerful analysis-ready geospatial data with high-dimensional embedded vectors, its applicability for crop classification is limited and cross-regional transferability remains untested. This study evaluated within- and cross-regional performance of crop classification using AlphaEarth across three cool climate agricultural regions: Northern Europe (Germany), Northern Japan (Hokkaido), and Northern US (Michigan). Within-region crop classification achieved high overall accuracy (91.4-99.1%) irrespective of regions and classifiers (support vector machine, random forest, and partial least squares). However, cross-regional transfer showed limited success. While models trained using Japanese dataset exhibited high accuracy (88.0-94.9%) in US dataset, reverse transfer (i.e. trained with US dataset and tested with Japanese dataset) and other combinations of transfer did not result in accurate classification. This study demonstrated (1) the utility of AlphaEarth as input data for regional-level crop classification, and (2) the limitations of AlphaEarth for cross-regional crop classification.

title: 83.Risk assessment of pesticide residues in dates in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi.
abstract: Pesticides are applied to protect plants from pest infestation and subsequent damage caused resulting in undesirable effects. Nevertheless, human exposure to residues from these pesticides may pose health implications. Residue monitoring programs have been established in many countries to assess the use of pesticides in accordance with good agricultural practices. The current study is an effort to report on the status of pesticide residues in date fruit and to conduct a risk assessment based on dates consumption among adults in the UAE. A total of 464 date fruit samples were obtained in 2024 as part of this survey in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and analyzed for 365 pesticide residues. Pesticide extraction was performed using the QuEChERS method, followed by detection through liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry. The results from the validation data indicate that the method has sufficient accuracy for the detection of pesticide residues in date plan fruits. A total of 292 (63%) samples did not contain detectable quantity of pesticides while 172 samples (37%) were found to contain pesticides exceeding the regulatory limits. Deltamethrin of pyrethroid family was the predominant insecticide found in 41% of the positive samples. In addition, residues of Cypermethrin, Pyridaben, Lambda-Cyhalothrin, Chlorpyrifos, Spirodiclofen, Thiamethoxam, Carbendazim, Imidacloprid, Fenzaquin, Fenvalerate, Matrine, Chlorantraniliprole, Clothianidin Fenpyroximat, Acetamiprid, Abamectin, Acirnathrin and Ethion were also detected. The hazard index data indicates that the dietary exposure to the assessed pesticides is within acceptable safety limits. The study emphasizes the significance of regular monitoring and its value in food safety management.

title: 84.Sustainable intensification and the land sparing mechanism.
abstract: The analysis of the malagasy "land rebound effect," conducted using an ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression model and panel data of 27 countries on World Bank time series data from 1990 to 2022, quantitatively demonstrates the relationship between agricultural value added and the expansion of cultivated land areas. The findings suggest three priority interventions: contextual adaptation of technologies through participatory approaches, strengthening land tenure security via formal certification tools, and building the capacities of local producers including training, financing, and economic diversification. However, there are methodological limitations due to the lack of detailed data on land dynamics and institutional constraints within rural communities, calling for complementary field studies to ground the econometric analysis in territorial realities.

title: 85.Spatially explicit negative prognosis of Cercospora leaf spot epidemics by process-based integration of leaf area index from remote sensing.
abstract: Crop production faces increasing constraints in managing biotic threats due to fungicide resistance, regulatory restrictions, and social pressures. While European farm chemical use requires justification, in-field spatial variability can lead to inaccurate assessments. We demonstrate the benefits of "episensing", linking remote sensing estimates of leaf area index (LAI) with a Cercospora leaf spot (CLS) epidemiological model for sugar beet (Beta vulgaris). We developedcercospoRa, an R package implementing a weather-based negative prognosis CLS model that requires canopy closure dates for initialization. We compared the conventional approach providing a single earliest estimated epidemic onset (EEEO) date for an entire field with an automated pixel-wise episensing workflow. To generate spatially explicit prognosis dates, we integrated a radiative transfer model with the CLS model, comparing uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) and Sentinel-2 (S2) imagery for estimating LAI and determining canopy closure dates. A General Additive Model confirmed that thecercospoRapackage successfully performed negative prognosis 21 das (days after sowing) earlier (μ̂UAS= 135.2 das, SE = 1.3) than the observed epidemic onset (μ̂observed= 156.9 das, SE = 0.4). Spatial analysis revealed greater variability in predicted onset dates from higher resolution remote sensing products (SDUAS= 12.5) compared to low resolution products (SDS2= 8.8). These results demonstrate that an episensing approach provide higher precision and automation capacity to provide greater spatial context by applying models at the pixel level, revealing spatial variability that classic field-scale or regional prognosis cannot resolve. Future improvements should consider additional variables and inoculum pressure for more precise epidemic onset definitions, alongside development of spatially explicit reference data.

title: 86.Developing a generic DSS model metadata catalogue and APIs for crop protection.
abstract: Decision Support Systems (DSS) in crop protection can give a helpful pest risk prognosis or recommendations for pest control, allowing farmers to make better-informed decisions. As a part of European Union policy strategy steering at the sustainable use of plant protection products, the EU H2020 project "IPM Decisions" created an online platform allowing farmers and advisors to access many DSS for major pests, weeds, and diseases in a variety of crops across Europe. The project has assessed and analyzed a set of research verified DSS's for integrated pest management. Information on the models employed by these DSS has been collected into a model catalogue, which is used by the IPM Decisions platform. Two Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) have been built to facilitate use of these models. In the spirit of the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reproducible) principles, the DSS API provides access to DSS models with their metadata, including the description of model input and output parameters. Weather API allows access to European on-line weather data sources and adapts their offering to the needs of the DSS models. The new APIs work as part of the IPM Decisions Platform, but they are publicly available so that also other agricultural software such as crop protection applications or farm management information systems (FMIS) can use them. In this article, we discuss the development of DSS and Weather APIs and present their structures and definitions. Finally, we present the services that DSS API and Weather API provide, and demonstrate the use of the APIs in three application cases.

title: 87.VITA: variational pretraining of transformers for climate-robust crop yield forecasting.
abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for global food security. However, current AI models systematically under-perform when yields deviate from historical trends. This issue arises from key data challenges, including a major asymmetry between rich pretraining weather datasets and the limited data available for fine-tuning. We introduceVITA (Variational Inference Transformer for Asymmetric data), a variational pretraining framework that addresses this asymmetry. Instead of relying on input reconstruction, VITA uses detailed weather variables as proxy targets during pretraining and learns to predict rich atmospheric states through self-supervised feature masking. This allows the model to be fine-tuned using only basic weather statistics during deployment. Applied to 763 counties in the U.S. Corn Belt, VITA achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting corn and soybean yields across all evaluation scenarios. While it consistently delivers superior performance under normal conditions, its advantages are particularly pronounced during extreme weather years, with statistically significant improvements (paired t-test, p ≈ 0.01). Importantly, VITA outperforms prior frameworks like GNN-RNN using less data, making it more practical for real-world use-particularly in data-scarce regions. This work highlights how domain-aware AI design can overcome data limitations and support resilient agricultural forecasting in a changing climate.

title: 88.Hybrid statistical-machine learning approach for analyzing legacy and new phosphorus losses from subsurface drainage systems.
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is essential for crop growth but leaches through subsurface drainage discharge, impacting water quality. This study's objectives are: (1) apply machine learning to quantify the contributions of incidental (new) and legacy (old) P in drainage discharge from an Organic CL site (primarily organic fertilizers) and an Inorganic BL site (inorganic fertilizers), and (2) evaluate the effect of manure application timing on P loss. We collected data from two on-farm sites in southeast Michigan, USA. We applied the Weighted Regression on Discharge and Seasons (WRDS) equation to analyze P load based on drainage discharge and fertilizer application timing. The data were divided into calibration and validation sets, and a machine learning algorithm was employed for training. The results showed strong model prediction performance. Organic phosphorus sources contributed 2-4 times more to new P loss than inorganic sources. When applied during winter months (Dec and Jan), organic fertilizer contributed to greater new P loss, whereas early fall applications (Oct and Nov) resulted in lower new P loss, showing the importance of application timing. At the Organic CL site, legacy P was the dominant contributor to total phosphorus (TP) and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) losses, accounting for 84% and 79% of losses, respectively.
