The interaction between irrigation and fertilization practices revealed that the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) management, specifically the treatment combining deficit irrigation and vermicompost, achieved 2.5 times higher water productivity than continuous flooding (1.13 kg rice m-3water vs. 0.41 kg m-3). Furthermore, under SRI, cumulative methane (CH4) emissions were approximately 10-39% lower than those from conventional treatments, peaking at 39% for the treatment combining deficit irrigation and vermicompost. This indicates the complementary advantages of SRI components. These findings suggest that SRI can be a practical climate-smart agriculture (CSA) technique when properly managed, enhancing water productivity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and improving rice yield sustainability.

title: 134.Transmission of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 to calves fed unpasteurized milk from experimentally infected cows.
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13 was confirmed in a dairy cow in Texas on March 25, 2024, by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) in response to a multi-state investigation into milk production losses. The amount and duration of virus shed in milk from the inoculated mammary quarters point to milk as a primary source of virus spread within and between dairy herds. Pasteurization has been shown to inactive the virus in milk, however, domestic cats consuming raw milk from affected cows developed fatal systemic influenza infection. Investigations on affected dairy herds demonstrated the presence of viral RNA in milk samples for up to 2 weeks before the appearance of clinical signs and diagnostic confirmation of infection. During this lag, unpasteurized milk may pose a risk to calves. Here, we sought to determine if H5N1 genotype B3.13 strain could be transmitted to calves fed unpasteurized milk from virus positive lactating cows. Five Holstein calves of approximately 7 to 11 weeks old were fed 0.95 L of unpasteurized milk twice a day via bucket. Milk was collected from two lactating Holstein cows inoculated by an intramammary route and fed to four calves for four days. Milk from two non-inoculated cows was fed to one negative control calf for four days. After four days all five calves were fed milk from non-inoculated cows. Calves fed infected milk showed clinical signs including nasal discharge, mild fever, mild lethargy, loose stool and slightly increased respiratory effort for 5-6 days. Signs of clinical disease were mild and may not be recognized under field conditions with other environmental or health stressors. Viral RNA was consistently detected in nasal swabs from all four calves from 2 to 4 DPI, with consistent detection persisting after calves were transitioned to being fed milk from non-inoculated cows. Infection was confirmed by viral RNA detected in nasal swabs, antigen and viral RNA detection in lung lesions, lymph nodes and pharyngeal tonsil, and seroconversion. Ct values of the nasal swabs were significantly correlated (-0.55) with lethargy in the calves. As Ct values dropped, and viral load increased, calves became more lethargic. Milk diverted from the human food supply in H5N1 positive dairy herds or from suspect cows should not be fed to calves without pasteurization. The determination of routes of transmission like the study described here is an essential first step to inform subsequent research on intervention and vaccination strategies.

title: 135.Direct and indirect cocoa deforestation in the tropical moist forests of Ghana.
abstract: Across the tropics, cocoa is one of the main drivers of deforestation. In Ghana, the world's second largest cocoa producer, the role of each of the main economic sectors in driving deforestation remains, however, contested - with cocoa, mining, logging, and plantations each blaming the others. Previous work has also suggested that food crops are displaced into forests by cocoa expansion, raising concerns about indirect land use change and impacts on food availability. Here, using satellite-based maps and secondary statistics, we quantify the direct deforestation drivers between 2000 and 2019 in the entire cocoa-growing region of Ghana. Then, we use a land-balance approach to assess the indirect role of the expansion of land uses in food crop deforestation. We find that cocoa is the major direct driver (~57%), followed by food crops and logging (~39% in total). Roughly 30% of the deforestation and degradation linked to food crops could be attributed to their displacement by other land uses - with 15% (9%-17%) due to cocoa expansion into food crops. In cocoa-saturated regions, indirect cocoa deforestation is likely to increase as forests only remain in gazetted areas, where growing food crops is either legal or more tolerated by officials than cocoa. Accounting for its direct and indirect role, cocoa is associated with ~20% of the deforestation in gazetted areas. This research highlights the need to move away from sustainability efforts targeting one single commodity at a time to more transformative approaches that develop a coordinated vision across the food and land system. Such a vision would regulate multiple commodities holistically, address lock-ins, and reconsider the overall goals of land systems in the region (how much land should be dedicated to cocoa, how and for whose benefits).
authors: Erasmus K. H. J. zu Ermgassen

title: 136.Estimating leaf nitrogen concentration of grain sorghum, corn, and forage sorghum with hyperspectral data and vegetation indices from a spectroradiometer.
abstract: Nitrogen deficiency in plants is often done by visual scoring. Spectroradiometers have been identified as a promising alternative to visual scoring because they can give information about plants' stress in the shortest time. Therefore, this study was carried out to identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum (EMS) that are related to leaf N and to determine how well we can use vegetation indices to estimate leaf nitrogen concentration (LNC). Conducted in a controlled greenhouse in Stillwater, Oklahoma, from August to October 2021, the experiment involved three crops grain sorghum, corn, and forage sorghum and four nitrogen levels (20%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of Hoagland's nutrient solution). The crops were grown in a split-plot design with controlled drip irrigation. Some crop physiological data, LNC, and reflectance data were taken. The results showed the possibility of using hyperspectral data to predict LNC with vegetation indices effectively estimating LNC. Among the indices tested, the Transformed Chlorophyll Absorption in Reflectance Index (TCARI) performed best, with an R2 of 0.72 in relation to LNC. Multiple linear regression (MLR) using the best vegetation indices (VIs) improved the estimation accuracy further, achieving an R2 of 0.77. These findings demonstrate that leaf spectral reflectance and vegetation indices can provide a fast, cost-effective way to monitor nitrogen status in bioenergy crops during the growing season. The study highlights the potential of hyperspectral reflectance to aid in precision agriculture by enabling rapid, in-season adjustments to nitrogen application, thereby improving crop management and productivity.

title: 137.Exploring methodological challenges in wetland valuation: a comprehensive review of global wetland valuation methods and applications.
abstract: The valuation of wetlands is integral to their conservation and sustainable management, yet methodological challenges persist in accurately assessing their worth. Drawing from diverse sources including the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands repository, EconPapers, Wetlands International publications, and databases such as Environmental Valuation Reference Inventory, this review critically evaluates existing wetland valuation methodologies and identifies key gaps in research. Market-based, non-market, and cost-based approaches are analyzed, highlighting their theoretical foundations, strengths, and limitations. Through a synthesis of literature, recurring themes and knowledge gaps are elucidated, providing insights into the current landscape of wetland valuation. Strategies for addressing methodological gaps are proposed, emphasizing the need for modifications to existing methods, integration of diverse valuation techniques, and further research and development. Examining global applications of these methods reveals challenges and opportunities influenced by socio-economic and cultural factors. Based on the review, recommendations are provided to enhance methodological rigor and practical application in decision-making processes. This comprehensive assessment underscores the importance of addressing methodological gaps for effective wetland conservation and sustainable development. Through collaboration and continued research efforts, the full value of wetlands can be accurately recognized and preserved for future generations.

title: 138.A comparative analysis of biochar's role in enhancing late-season growth and yield of cruciferous vegetables in coastal Bangladesh.
abstract: Coastal Bangladesh faces significant agricultural challenges due to saline soils, nutrient deficiencies, and environmental stressors, particularly during the late growing season. This study evaluates the comparative effects of biochar application on the growth and yield of cauliflower (Brassica oleraceavar.botrytis) and broccoli (Brassica oleraceavar. italica) under these conditions. Biochar, a carbon-rich soil amendment, has been shown to improve soil fertility, water retention, and salinity mitigation, making it a promising solution for sustainable crop production. Using a two-way ANOVA, the study examined the impact of biochar at four application rates (2, 4, 6, and 8 tons/ha) on key growth parameters, including plant height, leaf size, curd weight, and yield. Results revealed that while biochar significantly improved growth metrics across both crops, cauliflower demonstrated a more pronounced response in terms of yield and curd weight. Early-stage growth (15 days) showed transient improvements in leaf number, while leaf size and curd weight benefits persisted throughout the season. Interaction effects between crop type and biochar treatment were crop-specific, highlighting the need for tailored application strategies. This research underscores biochar's potential to enhance late-season growth and yield in coastal regions, offering critical insights for optimizing agricultural practices in resource-constrained environments.

title: 139.Genomic analysis of dry date palm fruit size traits and identification of candidate genes through GWAS.
abstract: The commercial value of economically significant fruits, including date palm fruit (dates), is influenced by various factors, such as biochemical composition and morphological features like size, shape, and visual appearance, which are key determinants of their quality and market value. Dates are typically consumed at the dry stage (Tamar), during which they exhibit a wide range of physical characteristics, such as color, length, weight, and skin appearance. Understanding the genetic basis of these traits is crucial for improving crop quality and breeding new cultivars. In this study, we integrated a genome dataset from highly diverse date cultivars with phenotypes of dry fruit such as length, width, area, and weight, identifying multiple significant genetic loci (SNPs) associated with these traits. We also identified candidate genes located near the associated SNPs that are involved in biological processes such as cell differentiation, proliferation, growth, and the regulation of signalling pathways for growth regulators like auxin and abscisic acid, as observed in other plants. Gene expression analysis reveals that many of these genes are highly expressed in the early stage of fruit development when the fruit attains its maximum size and weight. These findings will enhance our understanding of genetic determinants of fruit size particularly at the commercially important Tamar stage.

title: 140.Optimizing a protocol for salinity recovery during seedling stage in rice.
abstract: Salinity is one of the major abiotic stresses affecting rice production, but the levels of salinity in a given field are not constant across the growing season. Since the level of salinity stress a plant experiences can fluctuate, fast recovery from salinity stress may be a useful trait to improve rice productivity in salinity-prone areas. To develop a protocol to screen for salinity recovery, seedling stage hydroponic experiments were conducted to measure salinity recovery over time through both destructive and high-throughput image-based phenotyping. Seven rice varieties were included that had previously been classified as tolerant or susceptible to salinity. Following exposure to seedling stage salinity, plants were transferred to solution with no added salt and allowed to recover. Green leaf area and relative growth rates (RGR) of salinity tolerant varieties and one salinity sensitive variety initiated recovery (i.e. started to increase) after four days of salt stress removal and required six days to completely recover (i.e., to resume a similar RGR to that observed in the no-salt control treatment), while the other salinity sensitive varieties took more time to recover. Therefore, an optimal recovery period of six days after salt stress removal was identified for screening. Some salinity sensitive varieties were able to recover based on RGR and chlorophyll fluorescence values, while their Na+contents remained high. Therefore, salinity tolerance may not necessarily correspond to salinity recovery ability. The protocol optimized here can be scaled up to screen diversity panels and populations and used for genetic mapping of the seedling stage salinity recovery trait.

title: 141.Fungicide Efficacy and Climate Impact on Wheat Black Point: Experimental and Computational Insights.
abstract: The preprint "Fungicide Efficacy and Climate Impact on Wheat Black Point: Experimental and Computational Insights" has been withdrawn.

title: 142.Accuracy in agricultural citizen science: farmers' assessment of harvest output in Ghana.
abstract: This study investigates methods for farmer-led yield estimation in decentralized on-farm trials in Ghana. Decentralized trials are key to reaching remote communities and reducing costs, but often require physical presence during time-sensitive tasks. Farmer participation in data collection, especially if data can be shared digitally, may help overcome these constraints. Farmers' accuracy in measuring harvest output is often unknown, and therefore leads to falling back on technicians. This study determines the accuracy of farmer measurement outputs and determinants of the accuracy by using simple on-farm exercises in which farmers execute the estimation and measurement tasks. We tested yield estimation methods, including volumetric measurement and weighing of maize kernels and cocoa beans, to evaluate farmers' accuracy. Volumetric measurement, involving a container of known volume, proved robust and accurate without prior training, performing consistently across farmers with various education levels. Weighing with scales, while theoretically more precise, was error-prone, even after training, due to issues with scales and taring. Refinements such as using electronic scales and obviating tare adjustments could improve weighing accuracy. Volumetric measurement emerged as a practical solution, especially where training is limited, offering consistent results. The results of this study provide important information to researchers on the type and the magnitude of error that they can expect when farmers measure harvest output. Our findings suggest that decentralized trials relying on farmer measurements can expand trial reach, reduce geographical bias, and optimize resource use by decreasing reliance on technician visits.

title: 143.Combining mobile proximal soil sensors and a crop model to produce high spatial resolution yield prediction maps.
abstract: Precision agriculture requires a detailed knowledge of the within-field variation of yield forming factors and the productivity potential of each field area. Proximal soil sensing can effectively produce soil properties maps (e.g. soil texture), which combined with crop growth models, can be used to estimate the crop's needs at high resolution within the field. The goal of this work was to use a case study to test all the steps of the process of creating a yield map from mobile soil sensors and determine the impact of uncertainties and inaccuracies on the results. Soil texture maps (0- 90 cm of depth) of a field were derived from mobile sensors and used as input for the process based deterministic crop growth model HERMES to produce a high-resolution yield map. Compared to actual yield maps, the simulated yield map successfully identified the major differences in productivity within the field, although some spatial variation was lost during the simulation, mostly at the point of translating soil texture maps into soil water retention parameters. The model also showed a tendency of overestimating yield across the entire field. A crop model simulation based on measured soil parameters resulted in a yield prediction accuracy of about 10% higher than a simulation based on estimated (mapped) soil parameters. In conclusion: (a) the loss of heterogeneity, although measurable, occurred at a scale that might not have a significant impact on the site-specific management plan.; (b) most yield map inaccuracies can be attributed more to model calibration than to the mapping process itself.

title: 144.Growth, yield, and economic viability of Withania somnifera in agroforestry systems: a comparison of tree species in Charland, Bangladesh.
abstract: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) offers economic and therapeutic benefits in Bangladesh, enhancing farmers' profits and addressing the rising demand for natural health products. Its integration into woodlots and orchards can increase both income and productivity. However, research on its yield and economic viability in agroforestry systems with different tree species is limited, underscoring the need for further study. To reduce this knowledge gap, an experiment was conducted from June to December, 2022 in Char Kalibari, Sadar upazila, Mymensingh district of Bangladesh, aimed to evaluate the growth and yield ofWithania somniferaunder three tree species -Swietenia macrophylla(mahogany),Mangifera indica(mango), andCitrus sinensis(malta) - and to assess the economic viability ofWithania somnifera-based agroforestry systems in Charland (bars). A single-factor randomized complete block design with four treatments and three replications was employed, resulting in a total of 12 plots, each measuring 16 m2. The treatments consisted of T0, representingWithania somniferasole cropping (control), T1 asWithania somnifera-Swietenia macrophyllaagroforestry (WSAF), T2 asWithania somnifera-Mangifera indicaagroforestry (WMAF), and T3 asWithania somnifera-Citrus sinensisagroforestry (WCAF).Withania somniferaseedlings were transplanted into the interspaces, where the trees were permanently planted at a spacing of 2 meters (m) × 2 m. The results revealed thatWithania somniferain sole cropping had the best growth and highest dry root yield (692.0933 kg/ha), with significant differences in height, root length, and diameter compared to agroforestry treatments. Among the agroforestry combinations, the WSAF performed better than others, while the WCAF system showed the lowest growth and yield due to increased competition. Economically, the WMAF system provided the highest net income (3267.78 US$/ha) and benefit-cost ratio (3.38), making it the most profitable agroforestry combination. Correlation analyses indicated strong positive relationships between yield and key yield-contributing traits, such as root number, length, and diameter. In summary, the limited negative impact of tree components onWithania somniferaemphasizes the viability of its cultivation in agroforestry systems in the Charland area to meet national demand.

title: 145.Evaluating clinical mastitis in four dimensions: Part I. Defining the production, immunological, clinical and pathogen severity.
abstract: Assessing the severity of clinical mastitis (CM) is a critical step in making treatment decisions 26 and plays a crucial role in mastitis control and ensuring animal welfare. The prevailing method 27 for assessing the severity of CM mainly considers clinical symptoms. However, the severity of 28 CM can be assessed from various perspectives. This study aims to define and assess CM 29 severity in four dimensions: production, immunology, clinic, and pathogen. We collected data 30 on naturally occurring CM cases on three robotic dairy farms in Belgium (N = 2) and the 31 Netherlands (N = 1), involving four types of information: quarter-level milk yield, cow-level 32 somatic cell count (SCC), clinical symptoms, and causative pathogens. The final dataset for 33 analysis included 129 CM cases detected by the herdsmen from 105 cows and 113 lactations. 34 In the production dimension, CM severity was defined based on the maximum relative quarter35 level milk loss for the clinically inflamed and clinically uninflamed quarters separately. In the 36 immunological dimension, severity was defined based on the deviation of the cow-level SCC 37 from a cow-level baseline. The clinical dimension used existing scoring and stratified between 38 mild, moderate and severe cases. Finally, the severity in the pathogen dimension was based on 39 the bacteriological culture results of a milk sample collected from the inflamed quarter on the 40 detection day. For each dimension, scores between farms, parities, and lactation stages (LS) 41 were compared. A significant difference was only found between farms, both in the production 42 and clinical dimension. Combining the four scores may help to capture the full scope of CM 43 by simultaneously assessing the severity of cases across production, immunological, clinical, 44 and pathogen-related dimensions.

title: 146.Evaluating clinical mastitis in four dimensions: Part II. Correlation analysis between production, immunological, clinical and pathogen severity.
abstract: The severity of clinical mastitis (CM) can be assessed in four dimensions: production, immunological, clinical, and pathogen. Each dimension contains different information about the CM case. Both the level of severity in each dimension and their within-case correlation could help to get a thorough image of the disease. This information can be crucial to further substantiate and refine treatment decisions and understand the recovery process. This study aimed to investigate the correlations between these four dimensions of CM severity in a group of 129 naturally occurring CM cases at 3 farms in Belgium (N = 2) and the Netherlands (N = 1). To this end, we first performed an exploratory analysis by grouping CM cases based on their CM severity in one dimension and comparing the distributions of CM severity in the other dimensions. Next, the Spearman correlation matrix of CM severity between the four dimensions was calculated. Finally, to investigate the relations between severity dimensions among farms, parities and lactation stages (LS), we implemented linear fixed effect models. The severity dimensions exhibited positive correlations with each other, with Spearman correlation coefficients ranging from 0.3 to 0.5. The fixed effects models revealed that parity and LS have significant impacts on the relations between certain dimensions. For example, early LS exhibited different linear relationships between the immunological and production dimensions, suggesting that hormonal changes and energy distribution during this period may influence their associations. These results demonstrate that, although the CM severity scores in the four dimensions are positively correlated with each other, some variations exist between them.

title: 147.How do neglected and underutilised crops (NUCS) in Africa contribute to food security, nutrition and climate change outcomes: a scoping review protocol.
abstract: Building a more resilient food system requires growing crops that are adapted to variable environments- more heat, less moisture, greater pressure from pests and diseases, frequent extreme weather conditions like droughts and floods, inherently weak structured soils. Historically, plant breeding investments have been highly concentrated in cash crops and major staple crops like maise, wheat, and rice. Plant breeding investment in Africa has largely focused on the most economically important crops, like maise, tobacco, cotton, coffee, and cocoa, although some attention has been paid to legumes (including, cowpea and bambara groundnuts). Crops such as millets (i.e., sorghum, fonio, finger and pearl millets), which are utilised and most adapted to smallholder farmer's conditions, have not received as much investment as staple crops. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is one of the global regions with the least adaptive capacity to climate change. Current climate change predictions for the region paint a scenario of rising temperatures, increased variability in rainfall (change in patterns, onset and amounts) and increased frequency of extreme weather events such as drought, heat, combined drought and heat and floods. It is already experiencing some of these weather extremes with drought and floods ravaging most of SSA's landscape. Agricultural production is of particular concern. Small-scale producers in low- and middle-income countries are among those whose livelihoods are most vulnerable to climate change (Davis et al., 2022). The number of poor people dependent on agriculture and food systems in low- and lower-middle income countries is large-nearly 3.2 billion people live in rural areas, and most still depend to varying degrees on agriculture and food systems for their livelihoods (Lipper et al., 2020). Most of SSA's economies are still heavily dependent (directly or indirectly) on agriculture as a driver of economic and rural development. This is of great concern when viewed within the context of the impacts climate change will have on agriculture, and the vulnerability of rural households and the urban poor, regarding food and nutrition security, because the incidence of crop failure will likely increase. A healthy diet - one that prevents multi-nutrient deficiencies and excesses related to a variety of diseases - depends on consumption of a wide diversity of foods, including whole grains, legumes, nuts, fruits, vegetables, animal products, roots, and tubers. Notably, one of the key indicators of food security is the availability and accessibility of diversified food sources by individuals to meet their nutritional dietary requirements and enhance their healthy wellbeing (FAO; Chivenge et al, 2015). More recently, breeding of highly nutritious traditional, indigenous, and orphan crops has received increased attention. Some of the most micronutrient and protein-rich crops, like legumes, seeds, fruits, and vegetables, receive little-to-no breeding research and investment, but a diet incorporating a variety of NUCS offers improved nutrition and overall health, while also providing extra advantages for human productivity and livelihoods. This has led to heavy dependency on a few crops, lack of resilience in food systems, and an increase in dependency on commodity crops, as well as malnutrition and undernutrition.

title: 148.Advanced segmentation of soil constituents in X-ray CT images using nnUNet.
abstract: Segmentation of soil constituents in X-ray CT imagery is critical for advancing our understanding of soil structure dynamics, but challenges arise due to the overlapping X-ray attenuation. In this study, we explore the potential of nnUNet, a deep learning-based semantic segmentation model, for applications in soil science. We evaluated nnUNet on three challenging datasets: (1) heterogeneous soil structure with numerous material classes sharing gray value ranges, (2) fine roots in noisy images, and (3) permafrost core with gradual gray value transitions between sediment types. The performance of nnUNet was compared to other reference methods, namely ilastik, Rootine v.2 and manual thresholding. For Dataset 1, the segmentation accuracy surpassed that of ilastik for the particulate organic matter class. Dataset-specific challenges, such as annotating fine structures (Dataset 2) or poorly defined boundaries between material classes (Dataset 3), impacted the performance of nnUNet, compared to more specialized methods. The mean validation Dice scores were 0.71, 0.90, 0.92, for Dataset 1, 2 and 3, respectively, which suggested overall good model performance. Our study underscores that deep learning models like nnUNet perform well for the segmentation of complex soil structures and could assist the development of a generalized segmentation model, thereby fostering standardization in soil structure analysis.

title: 149.Addressing usability challenges to enhance data quality and efficiency in crowdsourced food system data.
abstract: Generating digitalized, mobile-phone-based data can transform food systems research. Challenges, including network accessibility, infrastructure, and reliance on users' basic digital literacy, and user familiarity with data-collection modalities, create usability issues that constrain user participation and data quality. Evidence of systematic usability research on mobile phone data-collection tools in development contexts is limited. Our study presents a mixed-methods approach for testing the usability of an unstructured supplementary service-data system, deployed on mobile phones in Rwanda. Combining heuristic evaluation and usability testing among eight respondents, we identified system-design and usability faults, and suggested fixes for system redesign. Issues identified included difficulties with starting and completing the survey; challenges in comprehending the question-and-answer format; and the constraints of users' low digital literacy. Comparing our results with those from previous data collection, we observed that the fixes statistically improved a dietary-recall survey response rate from 58% to 70% and reduced the number of low-quality responses from 24% to 11%, with the greatest improvements observed among female respondents. These results demonstrate how, with a moderate, up-front cost, integrating a relatively simple testing set-up into a design process can generate significant performance and output quality improvements. As mobile phones will remain the principal technology for data collection in lower and low- middle income countries, it is imperative that digital data collection system design is as intuitive, inclusive, and user-friendly as possible. Deploying human-centered design approaches can ensure this, and support generating high-quality, representative, and cost-effective data.

title: 150.Enhancing phytochemical composition and nutritional profiles in common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) varieties through roasting.
abstract: Common beans (Phaseolus vulgarisL.) are rich in protein and their combination of carbohydrates, dietary fiber, and minerals makes them a unique healthy food. This study examines the effects of oven roasting at 110°C for 70 minutes on the phytochemical content, antinutrient levels, phytosterols, and lipid profiles of 12 varieties of common bean (Phaseolus vulgarisL.) flours. Results revealed significant changes in phytochemical composition and antinutritional factors post-roasting, with notable variations among bean varieties. Stigmasterol and ß-sitosterol were the predominant phytosterols, influencing the lipid profile of both raw and roasted beans. Roasting conditions, including temperature and time, have a significant role to play in the stability and concentration of these compounds, suggesting the influence of heat-induced chemical reactions. Correlation analysis highlighted strong associations between phytochemicals, antioxidants, and nutritional components. The principal component analysis identified distinct clusters among bean varieties based on their phytochemical and antioxidant profiles, with pigmented varieties exhibiting enhanced nutritional content. These findings underscore the importance of understanding roasting's impact on common bean composition, informing strategies for maximizing their nutritional value in both dietary and industrial applications.

title: 151.Pedotransfer functions and their impact on soil water dynamics simulation and yield prediction.
abstract: Pedotransfer functions used to determine water retention parameters from more readily available soil 47 attributes (texture, soil organic carbon) may have a big impact on soil water dynamics and yield 48 simulations by crop models. In this study we used the model HERMES to quantify and understand the 49 impact of seven pedotransfer functions and two pedotransfer function ensemble models on crop yield 50 on sites with variable texture using water retention parameters (i.e. field capacity, wilting point and total 51 pore space) derived from the pedotransfer functions. Additionally, a continuous synthetic soil database 52 was created to assess the effect of gradual changes in soil texture on yield simulation. The accuracy of 53 the soil water dynamics simulations with the different pedotransfer functions was determined using soil 54 water measurements at the test sites. The impact of pedotransfer functions on yield simulations was 55 assessed by quantifying the yield differences at the experimental sites and across the synthetic soil 56 database. The choice of pedotransfer functions resulted in most cases in measurable differences in soil 57 water content dynamics, often showing a direct relationship between field capacity and water content. 58 Often, pedotransfer functions producing higher estimated field capacity also resulted in higher yield, 59 indicating that model yield simulation is sensitive to soil water availability. Pedotransfer functions 60 showed an increasing variability in water retention parameters estimation and yield simulation at 61 specific points in the sand percent continuum of the synthetic soil database, indicating that these 62 functions can be sensitive even to small changes in particle size distribution.

title: 152.The status of academic research on salmon farming: a scoping review protocol.
abstract: Salmon aquaculture (variously Atlantic and Pacific) has rapidly expanded across Norway, Chile, Canada, and Scotland, amongst others, driven by advancements in technology and market dynamics. However, this growth has spurred debates around environmental and socio-economic sustainability, especially concerning environmental degradation and "food imperialism." The intensive industry, once purported to be essential for global protein supply, is now scrutinised for prioritising luxury markets over food security and for its high ecological and social impacts, including pollution, disease spread, feed supply chain effects, and damaging livelihoods and standards of living. Climate change intensifies these concerns, with rising sea temperatures and extreme weather exacerbating disease and infrastructure risks, for example. Furthermore, the industry's reaction to activism raises issues of transparency and public accountability. With high mortality rates and substantial welfare concerns, the sector faces ethical scrutiny as well. This review aims to map academic research on salmon farming, analysing how studies address themes such as environmental impacts, socio-economic consequences, industrial profitability, and regulatory frameworks. We will search for relevant records from The Lens bibliographic meta-database using a tried-and-tested search strategy. We will then systematically screen records at title and abstract level and full text level according to a set of predefined inclusion criteria. Following this, we will systematically extract and code metadata, including geographical focus, study objectives and design, and funding sources. Visualisation tools, such as heat maps and interactive atlases, will illustrate research distribution and highlight gaps in the literature. The project will provide a comprehensive overview that will inform future systematic reviews and primary research, particularly in underexplored areas. This scoping review thus offers a foundation for a critical assessment of the research literature on salmon farming and its role in global food systems, social and ecological impacts, and the effectiveness of regulatory practices.
